sources.title: How QUITTR scaled a mobile app: copy onboarding, pay creators a revenue cut, and put volume first
sources.originalTitle: What Actually Works to Scale a Mobile App in 2026 w/ Alex Slater from QUITTR
sources.summary: Alex Slater explains how QUITTR scaled: copy the competitor's long onboarding instead of optimizing it, pay UGC creators a cut of ad revenue, and widen the audience with niche creative. He also covers news-style memes for cheap virality, and admits his costliest mistake was spreading budget away from Meta.

principles.text: Copy your leading competitor's onboarding instead of inventing one; they have already tested it.
principles.quote: if your idea is any good, it's probably been done before. That's like number one.

principles.text: Long onboarding works through sunk cost, but tweaking it only gains 5-10%, so spend time on bigger levers.
principles.quote: onboarding, just for the record, you can maybe find 5% 10% increase, like nothing really more drastic than that.

principles.text: Pay UGC creators a cut of the revenue their ads generate rather than retainers.
principles.quote: I think the best incentivization for UGC creators is a cut of ad revenue.

principles.text: To spend more on paid ads, expand your addressable audience with different creative styles aimed at distinct niches.
principles.quote: expanding your town. That is how you can spend more. And the way to expand your town is to make different styles of creatives.

principles.text: Memes need engagement and shareability, a simple message, and a serious cause, or they go viral without driving sales.
principles.quote: memes that could go viral, um and wouldn't drive any conversions cuz it's not serious.

principles.text: Reinvest in the channel that is working and push volume; don't spread budget to other channels too early.
principles.quote: had I just reinvested all the money that meta was bringing us back into paid we would be in a far different situation than we are today.

sources.title: Alex Slater on building Quittr: community accountability, social proof and approaching people
sources.originalTitle: App Mafia: Young Entrepreneurs Making $3,000,000/Month With AI Apps (Cal AI & Quittr)
sources.summary: Alex Slater, 19, founder of Quittr, joins the App Mafia founders to talk about how he went from broke in Miami to a community app doing about half a million dollars a month. He covers building on a taboo problem, accountability mechanics, learning from peers' proof, and making app building accessible.

principles.text: Seeing a peer succeed up close is proof you can do it too; use that proof to launch your own product.
principles.quote: Like I genuinely can. So I used that as proof as possible and then launched Quitter which helps guys stop jerking off and stop watching porn.

principles.text: Community-based apps win on accountability: put people with the same struggle together.
principles.quote: I think that's the number one thing with these like community based apps is just the sense of accountability.

principles.text: Target a taboo problem people won't discuss with friends by giving them an anonymous community and an app.
principles.quote: we're like, okay, like let's make a community. Let's make an app to actually help people quit.

principles.text: Gamify progress and make it public: streak-based rewards displayed in the community drive commitment.
principles.quote: We also give people like special orbs for how long they have they've stayed clean. So like 90 days you got a super rainbow orb.

principles.text: Reach out to people proactively; one cold approach to a stranger led to the connection that started his path.
principles.quote: I decide to approach and I go, "What's up, boys? Like, you guys want to get dinner? Like, what are some good places?"

principles.text: You don't need hard skills to start; the information is online, you just have to go find it.
principles.quote: all the information that you need to know to achieve the things you want is out there on the internet through GPT. You just need to go out and find it

sources.title: How a 19-year-old's porn-quitting app hit $250K/month: long onboarding, hard paywall, influencer distribution
sources.originalTitle: The 19-year-old Making Millions with His Ai Mobile App
sources.summary: Alex, Connor and Chris of Quitter explain how a porn-addiction app reached about $250K in a month within four months. The core lessons: a long diagnostic onboarding into a hard paywall, copying proven apps instead of reinventing, showing the app in every marketing video, and building a holistic product, brand and distribution.

principles.text: Use a hard paywall; free access kills engagement and commitment.
principles.quote: we did try that but the activity on the app dropped significantly no one used the app when it was free everyone used it when it was a hard pay wall

principles.text: Copy what top apps already do, then adapt it to your niche instead of reinventing.
principles.quote: we just studied the top apps that were making the most money and what we did is we screenshot every little bit of experience put it all in a figma

principles.text: Product, brand and distribution must all be strong; one weak area drags the whole thing down.
principles.quote: everything has to be holistic to be exceptional and to work fluidly if you're lacking in one area you're not going to kill the whole thing

principles.text: Show the app in marketing videos; views without product visibility convert poorly.
principles.quote: if you're going into marketing show the app in the video

principles.text: Build and ship now; don't procrastinate waiting for perfect.
principles.quote: don't procrastinate if you have an app idea and you have a way to do it just build it

principles.text: A single viral video proved virality's value, so optimize for it in scaling.
principles.quote: that one video with Jeremiah that reached $100,000 in a day that showed us how valuable virality is and so if we optimize for that

sources.title: How Alex Slater scaled Quitter to $500K/month: first-mover ads, influencer CPMs, copying winners
sources.originalTitle: He Made MILLIONS at 19 with His Ai App | Alex Slater w Founder's Formula
sources.summary: Alex Slater (20) explains how his anti-gooning app Quitter grew to 1.5M downloads and about $500K/month, and how App Mafia's course made $480K in three days. Useful on first-mover advantage, view-guaranteed influencer deals, reverse-engineering winners and volume. Much of the episode is lifestyle chat.

principles.text: Being first in a niche means no competition, easy conversion, and pricing power, plus cheap early ads.
principles.quote: We had the first mover advantage and so getting people in the door was really easy and getting people to pay for it was really easy because there's no competition. We can charge whatever we want.

principles.text: Reverse-engineer a proven app's monetization, paywall and influencer playbook, then replicate it in your niche.
principles.quote: I broke down exactly how they make money, exactly how they do the pay wall, exactly how they work with influencers, replicated it, and it worked.

principles.text: Pay influencers per view (CPM guarantees) so spend stays tied to results and you're almost always profitable.
principles.quote: we do view guarantees. So I think we pay around $2 uh CPM.

principles.text: Check an influencer's audience demographics before signing them, not just their view counts.
principles.quote: We got to look at the demographics always. That's like one of the prerequisites to like signing influencer.

principles.text: Volume is the lever: do more output per day and keep taking shots to make micro adjustments.
principles.quote: the most important part is volume. Double like double volume. Try to figure out to do two days of re two days worth of revenue one day.

principles.text: Knowing when you're wrong and killing an idea is a core founder skill, especially if it lacks marketing leverage.
principles.quote: one of the skills in being an entrepreneur is like knowing when you're wrong and knowing when to like bite the bullet sometimes and like call it quits.

sources.title: Alex Slater on scaling consumer apps to $400k+/month: drive, first sales and ad scaling
sources.originalTitle: He generates $400k/month at 19 years old with NO P*RN (Interview with Alex Slater)
sources.summary: Alex Slater explains why consumer apps pushed through influencers are a high-margin opportunity, how seeing a peer's results reset his sense of what was possible, and why he starts with the first sale and then scales ad spend fast. The rest is mindset: drive over curiosity, staying in an ambitious environment, and keeping the big picture in view.

principles.text: Software has near-zero distribution cost, so marketing is the only real cost and margins are high.
principles.quote: software has zero cost for distribution. This is almost pure profit. You only the only cost is marketing.

principles.text: Start with the first sale, then repeat it: 1 to 10 to 100 to 1,000. Don't anchor on millions while revenue is tiny.
principles.quote: Focus on getting the first sale. If you can get the first sale, you can get 10 sales. If you get 10 sales, you get 100.

principles.text: Once a channel works, test whether 100x the output gives 100x the return.
principles.quote: if you make money in one channel, if you did 100x the output, could you make 100x more?

principles.text: Keep the big picture in mind when choosing a product, but don't let huge targets kill your motivation.
principles.quote: Don't think about millions a month and then you have $10 in revenue. That's just going to kill your motivation.

principles.text: Scale ad spend aggressively and quickly once a channel is working; slow scaling is a missed opportunity.
principles.quote: We're scaling Twitter budgets uh daily spend on ads by 20% a day and in 3 days we should hit a million a month.

principles.text: Drive matters more than curiosity; curiosity without the drive to actually do it gets you nowhere.
principles.quote: I think drive is is more important than curiosity

sources.title: How Alex Slater and Connor McLaren scaled Quitter: pricing, influencer deals, ads and AI-built apps
sources.originalTitle: Scaling Beyond Influencers: From Rags to Riches w/ Alex Slater and Co-Founder Connor McLaren
sources.summary: A live Q&A with the Quitter founders on scaling a consumer app past influencer marketing. Alex covers pricing for volume, validating ideas via competitor revenue, shipping fast with AI, retention through community, and moving from organic to paid ads as revenue grows.

principles.text: Lower the price to win volume: more users paying less beats fewer users paying more.
principles.quote: it's not about how much you can make per paying User it's about the volume of users you can get to pay for a smaller amount that actually results in more Revenue

principles.text: Validate ideas by copying proven competitors' revenue; a known market gives confidence to build.
principles.quote: knowing that the top app makes 100K a month gave us the confidence to believe that yes this is a business and it can work out

principles.text: Squeeze the paywall: capture emails and push discounts to the ~85% who don't convert.
principles.quote: 85% of our users do not convert on the initial payall which is an important number because if we can push emails and discounts to that 85% of people that aren't converting maybe 10 or 20% of them will convert

principles.text: Match channel to stage: ASO and organic first, then ads once you can allocate budget at scale.
principles.quote: 0 to 10K a month is basic ASO and some organic post and then when you get to a million 5 million 10 million a month that's ads pretty much

principles.text: Build fast with AI; launching an app in days is realistic if you focus.
principles.quote: you can build any app any AI of your dreams in two three days and you can get it launched at the end of this week

principles.text: Community drives retention and creates a moat that clones can't copy.
principles.quote: communities are the best thing for retention

sources.title: Soar vlog ep. 1: stunts, branded cars and mind share to reach 100,000 San Franciscans
sources.originalTitle: How We're Building a Billion Dollar Company (Episode 1)
sources.summary: A chaotic vlog of the Soar team spending a big marketing budget on stunts in San Francisco: branded cars, hackathon sponsorships, QR flight credits and press-bait tweets. The useful ideas are building mind share through memorable stunts, documenting it, and pairing hype with a fast product.

principles.text: Use stunts to build brand mind share so people try the product when they need it; a good product keeps them.
principles.quote: Everyone's going to know about the brand for mind share. Anyone needs to book a flight might try us. They try us and they like us, they'll stay.

principles.text: Document the stunts as content so viewers discover, try and share the brand.
principles.quote: And then also documenting it. You know, if if someone gets into startups and they watch these vlogs, they're going to see the brand, they're going to try it, they're going to follow us

principles.text: Enough attention on the brand plus a good product is what matters, not where you are based.
principles.quote: You get enough eyes on the brand, you have a good product, like that's all that really matters.

principles.text: Branded physical assets make the company recognizable at events and hackathons.
principles.quote: Like we can now go into hackathons or events and they'll see the logo and be like, "Oh [ __ ] you're the Soul guys."

principles.text: Make the product claim tangible and exaggerated, like racing booking speed against a car.
principles.quote: It's like book flights faster than this car, you see?

principles.text: Offer risk-free incentives and play for press pickup that earns free mind share.
principles.quote: If you win, you get 25. If you lose, you lose nothing. There's no risk here.

sources.title: App Mafia: why consumer AI apps win with influencer marketing and lean teams
sources.originalTitle: These kids make $50M / Year in their 20s with mobile apps - App Mafia
sources.summary: The App Mafia founders (RizzGPT, UMax, Cali, Quitter, about $50M combined revenue) explain why AI plus easy builds plus influencer marketing created a new consumer app wave. They also cover lean teams, high-agency hiring and when a personal brand is worth it. The transcript has no speaker labels, so attribution to Alex is best-effort.

principles.text: The new app wave stacks three trends: LLMs, easy-to-build apps, and dropshipping-style marketing.
principles.quote: Every single sort of new player in this game that we play in um is leveraging at least two of those, usually all three.

principles.text: LLMs let you embed real functionality in single-player apps that incumbents founded in the early 2010s never updated.
principles.quote: With Chat GPT and at LLM's you can embed incredible functionality into a single player product.

principles.text: Apps built on a good product need little upkeep, so a lean team with a solid marketing system can run at over 50% margins.
principles.quote: if you build a good product, you don't have to maintain it. The code continues to provide the service on its own

principles.text: Influencer deals work when the contract guarantees views, and big-following creators beat random micro-influencers.
principles.quote: there's a lot of things we do in the contract to ensure that we get a certain number of views, etc., which allows it to be profitable.

principles.text: Hire high-agency people who are better than you in a field, give them resources and let them run.
principles.quote: the best people to have on a team, the A players you want on a team are people that are smarter than you, better than you in a specific field.

principles.text: A personal brand is an option, not a rule: it depends on whether your product's success relies on distribution.
principles.quote: I just generally disagree with oneizefits-all prescriptions

sources.title: Getting people to care is the hardest part: lead with the user's transformation, not your product
sources.originalTitle: getting people to care is the hardest part (marketing lesson)
sources.summary: Alex argues the hardest part of launching anything (apps, music, art) is getting people to care, not making it. He says image and inspiration drive attention, and marketing should centre the user's better future rather than "download my app." Persistence through early indifference is key.

principles.text: Getting people to care is harder than building the product; most launches fail on attention, not quality.
principles.quote: Getting people to care is the hardest part. Everyone has so much going on with their life. Why would they care about you and what you've released?

principles.text: Early silence is what kills most ambitions, so expect it and don't read it as proof you aren't good enough.
principles.quote: they start to think like I'm not good enough or this is so hard or like am I delusional, am I crazy, this that the other and they maybe give up.

principles.text: For creator-led products, your personal image and lifestyle drive whether people care about your work.
principles.quote: If I'm just a young guy in London making exceptional music, I dress well, I smell good, I drive a nice car, my captions on Instagram are on point

principles.text: Match your public persona to the audience you want to reach, even if it means not tying your name to what you love.
principles.quote: I can't tie my name too much to software. Even though I love it, I can't tie my name too much to software.

principles.text: Put the user first in all marketing: show their life could be better, instead of asking them to download your app.
principles.quote: Instead of being like download my app, you're like transform your life. These are very different things.

principles.text: Inspire people to sell to them, and stay persistent and consistent through being ignored on day one.
principles.quote: If you can inspire someone, you can sell to them.

sources.title: Alex Slater's 2025 lessons: run real numbers, scale Meta ads, post imperfectly
sources.originalTitle: 6 lessons i learned the hard way in 2025 (don't make my mistakes)
sources.summary: Alex reflects on 2025 at Quitter Aid: $4.2M revenue but far less cash because of loose spending, and a year of underinvesting in Meta ads while paying underperforming influencers. He also covers posting before it's perfect and mindset.

principles.text: Run the real numbers; big revenue doesn't mean you're rich.
principles.quote: Don't run the math in your favor. Don't say to yourself, "I'm making X amount a month, like I can do whatever the [ __ ] I want." Like, run the [ __ ] numbers and know where you're actually at.

principles.text: Subtract ad spend, team costs and platform cut from daily proceeds to see what's actually left.
principles.quote: 7K minus 3.5. Then there's team costs. So monthly team overheads divided by 30. And then that number is like you take that away from the 7K. You have Apple's cut.

principles.text: Don't copy what everyone on Twitter does without checking it fits your business; move budget to what performs.
principles.quote: We were spending money on influencers even though they weren't really performing because that was the game everyone else on Twitter was playing with no like self-realization on whether that was even the right thing to be doing for our business, which it wasn't.

principles.text: Scale a working paid channel: doubling Meta budget lifted proceeds to ~$15K/day.
principles.quote: it was as simple as just doubling the [ __ ] budget on Meta. Like, we should have done this ages ago.

principles.text: After scaling paid ads, improve creatives and diversify into SEO and Google search ads.
principles.quote: If we just keep putting more and more budget into ads and if we keep making the creatives better and if we start diversifying into SEO and and and Google search ads, we will be hitting 234 million months very very soon.

principles.text: Post without waiting for perfect; audiences move on if you go quiet.
principles.quote: People follow you for a reason. If you don't post, they don't really notice. They don't really care. They have other accounts they can consume from.

sources.title: Saw's $1M marketing month: attention stunts, one-tap booking and fighting card fraud
sources.originalTitle: We spent $1,000,000 on marketing in 30 days.. (Episode 2)
sources.summary: A vlog from inside a 20-year-old founder's flight-booking startup during a heavy marketing push. Alex explains positioning against commoditized airlines, the one-tap Tesla analogy, spending investment money on attention stunts, and a fraud problem that came with sudden growth. The creator-sponsorship playbook is mostly described by his YouTube head, Nathan.

principles.text: In a commoditized market, win on experience even if margins shrink.
principles.quote: No one's innovated. Everyone's too scared to because the margins on flights, they're very low. They're commoditized, but like I see a world where even if we make less money, we can still be the best.

principles.text: Incumbents profit from friction and upsell confusion; removing it is your wedge.
principles.quote: Airline companies, they make money by confusing you with the upsells, the multiple pages. That's how they make money.

principles.text: Cut the purchase flow to the fewest taps, like Tesla did for online car buying.
principles.quote: It's just one tap, find the flight book, enter code, it's done.

principles.text: Monetize through small add-on fees and expand into adjacent categories rather than inflating prices.
principles.quote: If if we charge like a small fee on bags and seats and then maybe we get into hotels, I think we'll be we'll be fine.

principles.text: Spending investment money on attention-grabbing stunts is justified if it earns attention.
principles.quote: We spent some investment money on it. And hey, look, it it gets the attention. So, job well done.

principles.text: Fight fraud with targeted checks, not blanket country bans that would block legitimate customers.
principles.quote: can't just ban Acura because longterm someone's actually going to have a real flight from there and that's not good.

sources.title: Day in the life of an app founder: creative-led Meta ads, CEO focus and building for the exit
sources.originalTitle: a typical day in my life as a million dollar app founder
sources.summary: Alex Slater vlogs a typical CEO day at his app Quitter: checking ad spend and revenue, managing the team, and hiring creatives and a CPO. He explains why Meta ad creative is the biggest lever, why equity and exits matter more than monthly cash, and what he learned from taking sole leadership.

principles.text: With Meta ads, creative matters far more than targeting settings; the algorithm finds the audience from the creative.
principles.quote: I think a lot of the specific Meta Ad settings don't really matter. It's all about creative nowadays.

principles.text: Expand your addressable market with new angles and creator styles; changing the creative changes who Meta shows it to.
principles.quote: All we need to do to target those demographics is to change the creative. Then meta will show it to those kind of people.

principles.text: Scale creative volume by building a creative team: a creator campaign plus a creative director for high-production videos.
principles.quote: our number one focus at Quitter right now is hiring a creative team.

principles.text: Growth comes from combining more varied creatives, more spend and fixed attribution.
principles.quote: if we expand our town with more different style creatives, if we throw more money at the system, and if we fix our attribution, we will be flying

principles.text: Aim for brand and equity value and a big exit, not just monthly cash take-home after marketing spend.
principles.quote: It isn't really cash it's the big exits, the equity value.

principles.text: One clear leader beats split 50/50 responsibility; talk to every employee daily so direction and hiring needs are clear.
principles.quote: Ever since I've kind of taken lead, I talked to all my employees every day. I understand exactly what's going on.

sources.title: How Alex Slater scaled Quitter: Stripe paywall to skip Apple's fee and 20% daily ad spend increases
sources.originalTitle: a week in my life as an app founder in miami
sources.summary: A Miami vlog week where Alex Slater, founder of the Quitter app, shares two concrete growth levers: a Stripe web paywall that avoids Apple's cut, and raising ad spend 20% a day while profitable. He also covers bringing in an experienced investor, cutting operational waste, and choosing a high-energy location.

principles.text: Route eligible users to a Stripe paywall to skip Apple's ~30% fee and lift proceeds without growing gross revenue.
principles.quote: It was more like 30%. But that's the fees that we would pay to Apple that we're now negating and uh just taking the cut through Stripe.

principles.text: Roll out a new monetization path as a small test (10% of users) and expand only once data shows it's more profitable.
principles.quote: Right now it's just a 10% test. So 10% of users see the strike pay wall. you know, as we get the data back and as we see it's like way more profitable, we're going to uh introduce it to everyone.

principles.text: Scale ad spend by 20% a day as long as it stays profitable, tracking gross versus proceeds after platform cuts.
principles.quote: boosting ad spend by 20% a day on the note that it's profitable. Like if it remains profitable, this number should jump by 20% every single day.

principles.text: Bring in an experienced investor or advisor when they can tell you what to focus on and save months of guessing.
principles.quote: it's easier for someone with more experience to come in and like tell you what to focus your time on rather than you guessing and trying to figure it out yourself.

principles.text: Audit operations regularly and cut waste fast; shutting down bloat as soon as it appears is a relief and unlocks growth.
principles.quote: it feels very relieving to finally cut it out and to see it and to like shut it down as soon as it pops up.

principles.text: Optimize for speed over comfort: choose the environment that keeps you moving fast rather than slowing your plans down.
principles.quote: Rather like move fast. Why be the horse when you can be the Ferrari?

sources.title: How Alex Slater got an app to $500k/month at 19 and the plan to scale it
sources.originalTitle: i was broke a year ago, now i live in a $10m mansion. (i'm 19)
sources.summary: Alex Slater reflects on going from broke to a Miami mansion in a year, building Quitter to about $500k/month. He explains the simple influencer-led app playbook, why scaling is the hard part, and how he plans to break the plateau by focusing on volume inputs and outputs.

principles.text: App playbook: build something valuable, pay influencers with cult followings to push it, reinvest sales into more distribution.
principles.quote: You build an app that's valuable that you would pay for that actually works. Okay? You then find influencers in your niche that have a cult-like following that would push your app within their videos.

principles.text: Making money from an app is easy; scaling and systemizing is the hard part, especially with team, ad spend and Apple's cut.
principles.quote: The hard part, I don't think, is making money, profiting. The hard part is scaling, becoming like systemizing things, and like yeah, like scaling beyond your mindset.

principles.text: To break a revenue plateau, stop chasing the big number and focus on inputs and outputs, i.e. triple daily volume.
principles.quote: I'm just thinking about the output, the inputs and the outputs because there are there is a certain amount of views that amasses the 10 or 15k a day we're doing right now

principles.text: Viral stunts, more influencers and more ads together kept the system flowing and drove the 500k/month.
principles.quote: We did a hell of a lot more influencers, a hell of a lot more ads and we just kept this like system flowing and that just resulted in the 500k a month.

principles.text: Go beyond selling the app: shift culture so the mission itself is the draw, gamifying and branding the product.
principles.quote: I want to shift culture. I want to make it cool to like quit watching pornography.

principles.text: Don't quit; enough volume makes failure unreasonable.
principles.quote: do so much volume that it would be unreasonable to fail. And I think if you just don't quit, you can't fail.

sources.title: Alex Slater on Quitter: stepping back, firing the team, and revenue rising anyway
sources.originalTitle: things are going really well ($150k first week back)
sources.summary: Alex Slater updates on Quitter after 20 days back: steady $9-10k proceeds days, rising LTV and ARPU, after he cut a 14-person team. He explains how he tests whether he is the bottleneck, works directly on paywalls and content, and holds a high bar on his own content.

principles.text: Step away from your company to test whether you are the bottleneck.
principles.quote: I took a step back to see if I was the issue. Um spoiler, I wasn't the issue.

principles.text: A bloated team can be dead weight; cutting headcount can raise revenue rather than lower it.
principles.quote: we fired everyone and the revenue went up. It didn't go down, it went up.

principles.text: As founder, work directly on the paywall and the content, improving them to your own taste.
principles.quote: getting behind the scenes looking at the pay walls improving them based on what I want

principles.text: Make content you yourself want to watch.
principles.quote: going into the content and making content that I want to watch

principles.text: Track unit economics like LTV and ARPU as the real signal of health.
principles.quote: consistent 9 to $10,000 proceeds days

principles.text: Hold a high quality bar and skip posting mediocre content, even if it is ready to ship.
principles.quote: I'm just not content with mediocre content.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Slater explains how QUITTR scaled: copy the competitor's long onboarding instead of optimizing it, pay UGC creators a cut of ad revenue, and widen the audience with niche creative. He also covers news-style memes for cheap virality, and admits his costliest mistake was spreading budget away from Meta.

chunks.heading: Copying beats inventing, and onboarding is a cheap lever
chunks.text:
- Alex's rule: "If your idea is any good, it's probably been done before." He assumes competitors have already A/B tested and are running the best version.
- QUITTR's onboarding was copied from the leading competitor, Brain Buddy. He advises anyone early or mid-stage to do the same and leave A/B testing until they are big enough.
- The same applies to ads. Coming up with new ideas is one of the worst things you can do. Change one small thing about something that already works instead of starting from scratch, "because when you start from scratch, who knows what works."
- Long onboarding works because of the sunk cost fallacy. Gamblers are not addicted to winning; they want something back for the time they spent. A user who has answered many questions is more likely to buy when the paywall appears.
- QUITTR's onboarding reached about an 85% paywall rate, and it has never been A/B tested, even now.
- Onboarding tweaks usually find only a 5-10% gain, and Alex says tinkering often hurts the app. At a thousand dollars a month, 10% is a hundred dollars, so bigger levers deserve the time.

chunks.heading: Creative is the main paid ads lever, and volume decides scale
chunks.text:
- Alex says the most important factor in paid ads is creative, once everything is plumbed correctly.
- A high-quality creative pipeline at a steady cadence separates an account spending 20k a month from one spending 200k or 2 million.
- At 20k a month, a few lucky creatives are enough. Getting from 200k to 1-2 million needs a pipeline that brings in diverse creative from many sources.
- Typical sources at scale:
  - a creator program (QUITTR's UGC program)
  - several creative agencies at different levels
  - in-house production
- Meta shows each creative to the exact person it suits, using the same targeting as Reels. Feeds differ so much between people that no general creative strategist knows what works, so diversity is the lever.
- Alex's general summary: "the only thing that matters is volume." A $2-3k/month app that did a week's worth of volume in one day could add real revenue for the month.
- QUITTR at 100k versus 500k a month: "we spent five x more, we did five x more volume. That's the difference." His closing advice: don't overcomplicate it, stop reading Twitter, and lock yourself in a box and figure it out.
- Questions like which colors or what size are noise. A person asking them is focused on the wrong things.

chunks.heading: Expand your TAM with different creative styles
chunks.text:
- Alex learned from people pushing around a hundred million a year in e-commerce that expanding your addressable audience is how you spend more.
- Do it by making different styles of creative for different audiences.
- Example he plans for QUITTR: a creative director tells UGC creators to make Muslim-niche Reels. They are shown only to that audience, so they don't affect the broader brand, and they open a new segment.
- Meta Ads and the ad library are most useful when creatives are as different as the audiences they serve.

chunks.heading: Creator programs: pay a cut of ad revenue, not retainers
chunks.text:
- Alex sources creators through a platform called Tribe, using a set reward to attract applicants.
- Best incentive in his view: a share of ad revenue. QUITTR and Cali AI both introduced this recently.
- The deal: a freelance creator sends videos, the team runs them on Meta, and the creator earns 10% of the revenue the ad generates.
- Example: if 10k is spent on an ad because it performed, the creator gets 1k. That is low risk for the app and high reward for the creator, and the more a creator earns, the more they have made for the app.
- He doesn't think retainers are smart.

chunks.heading: Memes and cultural moments for cheap reach
chunks.text:
- Alex hired a head of memes and calls memes an "untapped space." His view: "embed yourself in culture."
- Meta RevOps gives consistent revenue and perhaps 1.3x to 2x growth, with cash flow becoming an issue at scale, so he also chases big wins: 10-million-view influencer videos and memes.
- A meme needs high engagement and shareability, which comes from a simple message understandable in one read. His example: the "Quit Your Job buys OnlyFans and shuts it down" meme, which can be shared with friends.
- It also needs a good cause. A meme that goes viral but isn't serious (his example: renaming Epstein's island "Goonville") won't drive conversions.
- Things that announce news or sound like real news perform best.
- Memes get lower CPMs and fewer downloads than ads, but are far more likely to go viral.
- Alex's balance: serious enough to convert, shareable enough to spread.

chunks.heading: Meta account tactics: old ads, impressions filter, and install vs purchase
chunks.text:
- **Copy cautiously.** Most people copy a competitor's oldest running ad. Alex suggests the opposite for your own account: put your worst ads in a campaign at $5 a day and let them run forever, because the oldest running ads are your worst ads, which sends competitors down the wrong path.
- **Most-impressions filter.** It applies to larger ad accounts, so a relatively new account can avoid it. Awareness campaigns have much lower CPMs than conversion campaigns. Alex describes running an awareness campaign, changing the CTA from "learn more" to "download", so a competitor sees an app ad with many impressions and assumes it is good.
- **Push through lower-event funnel pain.** For nearly every new app, an install-optimized campaign is the most efficient by ROAS for two to three weeks and gets paying customers more cheaply than a purchase-optimized campaign.
- Teams often stop the A/B test too early. Alex says the purchase campaign has eventually taken the lead every time in accounts he has seen, but it needs money burned to warm up the purchase event so Meta learns who your exact buyers are.
- The ideal is paying a lot for a small number of high-intent users. If target CAC is $15, you pay $15 for a customer who converts every time. Click-through rate may look poor.
- His conclusion: don't over-index on hook rate, click-through rate or CPM. Worry about CAC, and keep the account on the purchase event through the early dip.

chunks.heading: Mistakes: agencies, spreading budget, and staying on what works
chunks.text:
- QUITTR burned over 100k on creative agencies while chasing organic reach. They promised around a thousand pieces a month and viral hits; it never happened and he regrets it.
- A bigger regret: after finding success on Meta, he expanded horizontally into influencers, UGC and organic before scaling volume on Meta. Budget was misallocated away from Meta even though influencers returned less. Had he reinvested Meta's returns into paid, he says he would be "in a far different situation."
- Advice: early on, scale Meta to about a million a month and focus on it. Then add TikTok, Google or DSPs, and Meta success makes those channels come online faster. Alex compares this to owning the S&P 500 first and diversifying later.
- Viral reach is not revenue. A video that reached over a million views and was retweeted by Elon led to no business, while boring Google Doc screenshots drove 30-40 new clients.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Slater, 19, founder of Quittr, joins the App Mafia founders to talk about how he went from broke in Miami to a community app doing about half a million dollars a month. He covers building on a taboo problem, accountability mechanics, learning from peers' proof, and making app building accessible.

chunks.heading: Alex's origin story and the "AI app" opportunity
chunks.text:
- Alex Slater (19, from the UK) dropped out of school at 17 and flew to New York alone to chase startups. His first idea was a failed attempt to raise $100 million pre-seed to build "the WeChat of America".
- At 18 he was nearly broke (about $500 left) and traveling the US. In Miami he approached a group at a hotel pool and ended up meeting Zach Yadegari. Zach was then building Cal AI with Blake Anderson.
- Alex used Cal AI's growth (50K, then 100K, then 200K, then 400K a month, roughly doubling monthly) as proof he could do it too. He says "I was with Zach at the beginning... I saw this go from nothing to something and I was like, I can do this too."
- He launched Quittr, an app that helps guys quit porn. About 12 months in it has about 1 million downloads, roughly 250K paying users and about $500K a month in revenue.
- His view of the opportunity: AI let small teams build products that weren't possible a few years ago, and social media made distribution easier. Combining the two is the macro bet.
- On being in an "AI bubble": he separates the foundation model layer from the application layer, where App Mafia sits. He compares it to the 2000 internet "bubble" that still produced durable companies.

chunks.heading: Building Quittr: a community-based habit app
chunks.text:
- Alex got into the idea from the self-improvement rabbit hole, where "stop jerking off" is a recurring piece of advice and a hard thing to follow through on. He says the topic is taboo, and people won't talk about it with friends.
- Core product mechanism: a community where users post streaks and how they feel. Members earn "orbs" for time clean, for example a "super rainbow orb" at 90 days, shown publicly next to every post. Accounts can be anonymous.
- His diagnosis of why it works: a community of people with the same struggle creates accountability. The sense of "we're going to quit together" is the main driver of community-based apps.
- Proof points he cites: about 30,000 five-star reviews, near-daily emails from users, and in-person thank-yous.
- He argues the real reach is the whole problem space (billions of people with the habit), and that many users are very young, which is part of why the app matters.
- He says the greatest inhibitors of success are vices, and that stopping heavy weed use (3+ times a day for 5+ years) was what let him find success.

chunks.heading: The App Mafia playbook: picking problems and building
chunks.text:
- Problem identification: find problems you or the people close to you experience. Do market research, identify the key pain points, then study what other apps in adjacent industries do and build a solution for the specific problem.
- Alex says the team cares about self-improvement, which shaped which problems they chose.
- Skills needed are lower than people think. He says he has IQ tested people he has worked with, and found even people around 100 IQ built very successful apps. His view: some baseline intellect is needed, but beyond that "it's really a problem of agency."
- Agency means finding the right information, assessing the core problem, looking at what worked in the past, using other apps as case studies, and rebuilding for a novel solution.
- Marketing in a sentence: identify the right creators, identify the right hooks for UGC, create content, put it out, iterate, double down on what works, drive people to the app, and provide value so you get paid.
- Everything in consumer apps is open source: download a competitor's app and you see its exact funnel. He says Cal AI's funnel and how it reached its revenue is visible to anyone who installs it, and revenue is verifiable on public databases like Sensor Tower.
- On learning to code: use AI as a tutor, not a copy-paste machine. Ask it to explain concepts (for example MVVM in SwiftUI, backend security, API calls, state management), implement, iterate and rewrite yourself. Copy-paste without understanding teaches nothing.
- On other copycats: tens if not a hundred-plus other apps make over $100K a month by rebuilding the experience for other domains. His examples are Quittr-style apps for sugar and alcohol, Cal AI-style apps for scanning supplements, and UMAX-style apps for tailored skincare.

chunks.heading: Fundraising vs. bootstrapping
chunks.text:
- Alex says all the App Mafia apps are bootstrapped. Investors reach out "all the time".
- Reasoning: the VC model fits companies chasing multi-billion outcomes. In their space the bottleneck "is not cash", it is insight, knowledge and agency. The difference between having $100K and $5K to start is "very low", mainly speed.
- He expects the group will likely raise for future, much bigger companies, but not for these.
- Why not raise: starting from zero teaches more than starting with a $250K check. Starting with cash lets you hire people to do everything and never learn the skill yourself, which in this space he thinks is a mistake: "you're actually kind of shooting yourself in the foot if you don't learn how to do the thing yourself."
- He says some funded apps raised millions and he questions what they spent it on.
- Group scale he cites: across App Mafia's portfolio of founder-built apps, they do over $70 million a year, not counting Bags (which he thinks could push it toward $100M+).

chunks.heading: Selling the App Mafia course and building a personal brand
chunks.text:
- The App Mafia course teaches how to scale apps. Structure: ideation, design, development and distribution, with over 10 hours of content, plus case studies updated roughly monthly.
- Price: $2,500 for access. Alex says there are no guarantees. Launch was set for Saturday, October 23 on appmafia.com (the domain cost about $10K).
- Why make it: they got DMs constantly from people trying to learn this, but never had the economic incentive to produce a structured course. They concluded the knowledge is a black box and they could push the industry forward by structuring it.
- Alex says they don't need the money. The main reason is leverage on personal brands: they plan to put all proceeds into ops, videography, the house, events and marketing for App Mafia to grow their personal brands, then use that distribution for hiring and future businesses.
- The group lives together in a house in Pinecrest, Miami (about $40,000 a month rent, described as a roughly $10M house). They plan to vlog about an hour every other week.
- He frames content as a skill to train like building apps: "we have all the recipes for success... it's a skill, the same way that building an app is a skill."
- Giveaway mechanic: one free course for a listener who DMs @appmafia_ on X and explains who they are and why they want it (and why they can't pay). He says they will give more free access to people who can't afford it.
- Alex's own proof point is that he and Connor saw what Zach and Blake did with Cal AI and ran the same playbook themselves.

chunks.heading: Views on AI and self-improvement products
chunks.text:
- Alex agrees AI is among the greatest technological developments in history and that it commoditizes intelligence (personal tutors, doctors, coaches).
- On whether AI dependence hurts social skills: he argues AI can act as a coach. Feedback on RizzGPT-style products showed people learned better flirtatious but kind responses themselves by watching how the AI recommended replying.
- Design principle on insecurity: the goal is "inspire action without creating insecurity". For UMAX face ratings, they set a floor of 55 out of 99, most users score 70+, and a potential score always sits 5 to 10 points above the overall one. Recommendations are basics like going to the gym, eating less calorie-dense food and washing your face. They avoid mewing, bone smashing and hormones.
- He rejects building judgments about competitors: "I like capitalism... the free market is a good thing", and says the best answer to bad information is better information (build Quittr) rather than policing others.
- Product philosophy: more people building software is good because competition makes products cheaper for consumers, and the new apps are tools for human improvement.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex, Connor and Chris of Quitter explain how a porn-addiction app reached about $250K in a month within four months. The core lessons: a long diagnostic onboarding into a hard paywall, copying proven apps instead of reinventing, showing the app in every marketing video, and building a holistic product, brand and distribution.

chunks.heading: How Quitter's onboarding and hard paywall drive conversion
chunks.text:
Alex Slater (19, product and dev, with Chris on design and Connor on growth) built Quitter, an app to quit porn. It reached about $250,000 in a single month, four to five months after launch. Alex's view: the best app and branding are wasted without a good onboarding flow. His flow:

- A 12-step quiz that doubles as a diagnosis (history of use, escalation, symptoms), so the user feels they are building their own plan.
- A symptom picker (low drive, no interest in girls, etc.), then testimonials, then a list of porn's side effects and the benefits of quitting.
- A review prompt before the user has used the app. Most skip it, but "a select few people just click five stars", which adds up.
- A personalised paywall card using the user's name: "Hey Alex, it's time to invest in yourself". Framing the price as an investment in yourself is deliberate.
- Mixpanel showed roughly 98-99% step-through on every onboarding step.

He sells the outcome, not features. The flow never explains the app's contents; users see the app through App Store screenshots, influencer content and ads.

chunks.heading: Why a hard paywall and a long onboarding
chunks.text:
- Quitter is a hard paywall at $12.99/month or $45/year, shown as "$20 or $12.99 a month". Many buy yearly, so cash comes in upfront and is reinvested into marketing.
- About 15% of downloaders convert.
- The team tried a free/premium model first. Activity on the app dropped significantly: "no one used the app when it was free, everyone used it when it was a hard pay wall".
- Paying creates commitment, so users value and use the product more.
- Alex claims that without the long onboarding and hard paywall they "wouldn't have had 99%" of today's revenue, and that a straight-to-product freemium version would have made maybe $10K.
- The length filters out unserious users; serious ones finish and pay. Too short fails.
- The flow works like a sales call: ask questions until the user tells you why they need it, then the sell is easy. He compares it to VSLs and landing-page quizzes.

chunks.heading: How they built the onboarding
chunks.text:
- Early on they studied the top-earning apps (those making $5-6M), screenshotted every step, lined them up in Figma, and ripped the pattern for their niche.
- He advises others to do the same, adapted to their own niche, rather than reinventing the wheel: "All these million dollar apps have done the research and testing for you."
- Superwall handles the paywall, so they can A/B test pricing and design on the fly. Superwall later used Quitter's paywall as a template on its site.
- Mixpanel tracks onboarding drop-off.

chunks.heading: Product design for retention
chunks.text:
- Started as a simple streak timer, then added a community, breathing exercises, 20+ tools, an AI therapist ("Melus") and a resources library.
- A panic button vibrates the phone and shows the user's own reason for quitting. A tree grows as the streak lengthens, and users don't want to cut it down. There are milestone badges and a recovery progress bar.
- On first entry users get a to-do list (journal why they quit, post in the community) to build retention. The community is the biggest moat: "the tools can become defunct but the community stays forever."
- Referral rewards ($5 per friend) brought few downloads because the product is too personal to share. Organic growth comes mainly from ranking first for "quit porn" style App Store searches.
- Cancellation or deletion triggers a feedback form feeding a feedback feed. Users who suggest an implemented feature get $100.
- Design: all black for a premium feel, DM Sans, and spacing and text sizes in multiples of 4 (8px from borders, 12/16/18 text). Alex says polished design makes people more willing to pay.
- The tech stack is Swift, ChatGPT-assisted coding, Firebase and Figma.
- They chose the name Quitter because "NoFap" was trademarked, and wanted the SEO benefit of an app name matching the movement.

chunks.heading: Influencer distribution and deal structure
chunks.text:
- The team started influencer spend with $3,000, which became $37K in the first month.
- Target creators in adjacent niches: religious (e.g. the devil and lust), fitness/testosterone, and self-improvement/semen retention. Each gets its own pitch angle.
- The pitch is the outcome, not the action: higher energy, confidence with women, becoming a man.
- Deal structure:
  - Four videos per month (Instagram and TikTok, so eight posts) with a view guarantee, e.g. 500,000 views for about $1,000.
  - Pay 20% up front and the rest after the views, funded by Apple's payouts, which is how the $3K was stretched.
  - If the creator misses the guarantee, they keep posting until they hit it, or the contract is pro-rated.
- Pricing uses an internal CPM of roughly $2-3, never shared with creators. The pitch is a flat retainer based on expected views; creators with egos need to be handled.
- Contracts include usage rights so the videos can run as ads.
- Ripped creator videos are the best-performing and cheapest ads.
- One viral video had 9.9 million views, doing $40K in a day and $100K over about 65 hours. That creator was paid $3 CPM for a guaranteed million views plus a bonus of a few grand.
- Attribution is hard since many people just search the App Store, so ROI is a back-of-napkin estimate.
- Videos must show the app. Videos with millions of views but no app shown brought in only about $2,000.
- He cancelled a roughly $10K contract because the creator only wanted a mention 1-2 minutes into the video.

chunks.heading: Outreach system
chunks.text:
- Message every creator through DMs, a consult call if they sell one (he paid about $50 for the first religious creator, and wasted about $150 on others), and email.
- Opening line is "paid promo", and they send from the verified brand account, which bumps the message in the inbox.
- Keep it short: who they are, the outcome, social proof (100,000+ users), and "reply or send your number".
- Don't state the price over message. Get them on a call, where they are in the moment and it's easier to say yes. A text gives them room to think and negotiate.
- Volume matters: the first 100 may not reply. A VA in Pakistan (found via Fiverr four years ago) sources creators into a Google Sheet and DMs them.
- Pitching also appeals to mission: helping people struggling with a problem in their audience.
- Many creators who beat porn addiction want to help others.
- Ops stack: Grow (creator contracts and payouts), Notion database, Zapier onboarding email, agree.com contracts.

chunks.heading: Scaling: paid ads, virality and brand
chunks.text:
- Sequence: influencers first to bootstrap, then paid ads (about $40K/month spend returning 3-4x ROAS), then organic. Friends make hundreds of thousands a month on organic alone.
- Next moves: larger creators and podcast sponsorships, church and diocese partnerships, comedy skits, and viral stunts. Having a 100K day from one viral video showed how valuable virality is.
- Purple branding is intentionally the opposite of the industry's orange.
- Possible stunts include throwing purple paint at porn conventions, or a satirical tweet about buying and shutting down PornHub.
- Alex compares this to Liquid Death-style brand building.
- Retention is not a focus yet: they sell mostly yearly plans, so churn matters less. The idea is to build authority with studies and neurologists, which could also support high-ticket offers.

chunks.heading: Advice
chunks.text:
- Everything must be holistic: product, onboarding, design and distribution all have to work together.
- The repeatable loop: pay creator, creator gets views, views drive downloads, downloads drive revenue, and revenue is reinvested into more distribution.
- Evaluate whether influencers actually exist in your niche (e.g. AI writing tools rely on organic faceless content instead). Test channels, then hammer what works.
- Don't procrastinate: "just go send DMs to 2,000 influencers, and the next 2,000 change it up."
- Make people problem-aware, then solve the problem.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Slater (20) explains how his anti-gooning app Quitter grew to 1.5M downloads and about $500K/month, and how App Mafia's course made $480K in three days. Useful on first-mover advantage, view-guaranteed influencer deals, reverse-engineering winners and volume. Much of the episode is lifestyle chat.

chunks.heading: Quitter: origin, idea selection and the product
chunks.text:
- Alex started Quitter a year before this interview. It helps guys stop gooning (quit porn), and he says it has 1.5 million downloads and about $500K in revenue a month.
- His reasoning for the idea: self-improvement culture had made it normal to question junk habits (TikTok, junk food, porn). He "saw a gap in the market" for an app that made quitting feel cool rather than taboo.
- The mission already had a built-in audience: the NoFap community on Reddit has millions of members.
- Product mechanics: he gamified it with orbs unlocked for streak length ("battle passes in Fortnite" style), plus a community of people with the same problem. Because the topic is taboo, talking about it openly makes it easier to deal with.
- First month was about $30K in revenue. He met co-founder Connor through the YC Co-founder Matching platform, then in person in San Francisco, after both had the same app idea.
- Before Quitter he built "Rich AI" with his brother Chris and dropped it. His reason: "there wasn't really much marketing leverage I could pull." He treats knowing when you're wrong and being willing to "bite the bullet" and quit as an entrepreneurial skill.
- He says he doesn't want to be known just for this niche long term, but thinks Quitter can reach $3M, $4M or $5M a month "not with much difficulty."

chunks.heading: Reverse-engineering a proven app instead of inventing
chunks.text:
- Core method: "the internet is beautiful because you can reverse engineer almost any business and any individual."
- For Quitter he used Cali (a calorie-tracking app) as the template. He broke down exactly how Cali makes money, how its paywall works and how it works with influencers, then replicated it, and says it worked.
- Same logic for a personal brand: he scrolled to the bottom of Drake's Instagram and moved up through the posts (30K likes, then 100K, then 200K likes) to see that "things start small then they blow up."
- If he went broke and had to restart (niche unknown), his plan:
  1. Study where money is flowing.
  2. Find the people making the most in a niche and break them down fully.
  3. Reverse engineer and launch his own version.
  4. Work very hard on on-the-ground marketing.
- Example of ground-level marketing from Quitter's early days: jumping into Reddit communities and posting "this app changed my life." He admits these were fake reviews, and says they generated thousands of dollars in the early days.

chunks.heading: How Quitter scaled from $30K to $500K a month
chunks.text:
- **$30K in month one:** no one had heard of the product, so he had first-mover advantage. With no competition, "we can charge whatever we want," and getting people in the door and paying was easy.
- **30K to 100K:** scaled operations and worked with more influencers.
- **Around $70K a month, December:** launched Meta ads. Because Quitter was the first quit-porn app running ads, he had "complete penetration" and about a 7x ROAS. He says they put in 30K the first month and then 30K x7 after that.
- ROAS then fell as spend scaled.
- **January influencer video:** a 15-second skit that he thought was bad. It went from $5K to 10K, 20K, 30K, up to 80K in revenue in one day. The skit: an influencer lying on a bed with lotion thinks about it, pulls out Quitter and stops.
- Revenue chart pattern: a consistent climb with about three or four days in total where it spikes sharply.
- He has been stuck around $500K a month for four or five months. He is restructuring because profitability dropped, after he reviewed the work of the person he had given full trust in running marketing for 12 months and "lost complete faith" in it. His view: marketing is the most important function because without it you can't generate revenue.

chunks.heading: Influencer deals and the scaling problem of a taboo niche
chunks.text:
- Payment model: view guarantees, about $2 CPM (about $2,000 per million views), tied to views so they are "almost always profitable."
- Check audience demographics before signing an influencer. This is "one of the prerequisites to signing" one (for example, a creator with 10M views a month where 8M are women is a poor fit for a male-targeted app).
- His framework: "Every business has a fundamental problem."
  - Quitter has high pain points, so people convert and pay well, but fewer influencers will tie porn to their name.
  - Cali is easy to scale because every gym influencer can promote it, but it faces accuracy backlash.
- Skit-style content worked well for Quitter because the creator doesn't need to claim personal use.

chunks.heading: Info products: App Mafia course and community
chunks.text:
- Alex launched a course and paid community with App Mafia, his first time doing info products. He is pro info products: you're selling information people can use to make money themselves, so it makes sense even if it looks scammy.
- Launch numbers: $220,000 in the first 24 hours, $160K the next day, $100K the day after, so about $500K in three days. He notes the profit margin is close to 100%.
- Why it worked: "it took years of building reputation."
- He says he is helping people go from about $2K to $10K, $20K or $30K a month.
- App Mafia: "the Milk Boys for entrepreneurship." Four co-founders in a Miami mansion vlogging team-10 style. They post both lifestyle vlogs (to inspire) and education. They released a 13-hour free app-building course at plug-atm.com ("no benefit from my end").
- Spending after the launch: course money was spent fast. He says half a million went in 44 days, on Instagram handles (about $100K), club tables (about $50K), rent (about $250K over three months), a private chef (about $10K a month) and food (about $5K a month), leaving about $20K.

chunks.heading: Software leverage versus service businesses
chunks.text:
- His argument for apps: "I'm making money sitting here doing nothing because people are downloading and paying." With an agency or sales-call business, "if I want to make 2,000 I have to go take an hour sales call," so you remain an employee of your own business.
- AI speeds app-building a lot: his roommate Blake built and launched an app on the App Store in 48 hours with AI, work that "usually takes several months."
- His view of the "$30K a month in info" plateau: it can keep you from the next level. If the goal is a very large outcome, "you're not going to get there if you play this mini game."

chunks.heading: Output, volume and mindset
chunks.text:
- Doubling income: "Double volume. Try to figure out how to do two days of revenue in one day. That's how you double your monthly income." More shots at the dartboard means more micro-adjustments.
- Value principle: provide value to one person and you get rewarded; provide it to a million people and you get rewarded proportionally. He ties his higher revenue to helping 1.5M people download his app.
- On mentality: "Just think you're the best and become the best, and have the humility to learn from your mistakes."
- His own routine: 7 to 8 hours sleep, gym, meal prep planned in advance. He says "listen to your body" on rest.
- He says he started in 2024: first 18th-birthday money was £10K from his dad, then a roughly three-month San Francisco trip, then Miami, where he met Zach (18, running Cali, about $3.5M a month).
- Hiring principle on delegation: he's waiting until he hits about $75K a month before hiring closers and setters, and notes closers and setters don't want offers making under $100K a month.

chunks.heading: Environment and personal brand
chunks.text:
- His advice for someone stuck: scrape together money to leave your environment. In a new place, "when you normalize it, it becomes more achievable."
- Surroundings matter: he declined to learn from someone driving a McLaren on finance who barely had liquid savings. He cites "surround yourself with the happy and lucky and you become just like them."
- He is building a personal brand (recent reels about 100K views each), is interested in music, and wants to move to LA (more cultured, "real wealth") over Miami, which he calls "a bubble."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Slater explains why consumer apps pushed through influencers are a high-margin opportunity, how seeing a peer's results reset his sense of what was possible, and why he starts with the first sale and then scales ad spend fast. The rest is mindset: drive over curiosity, staying in an ambitious environment, and keeping the big picture in view.

chunks.heading: Quitter and the consumer-app opportunity
chunks.text:
- Alex frames consumer apps as the new version of SMMA, crypto, trading and dropshipping. All of those were attention arbitrage, and apps are "a digital product" pushed through influencers.
- His case against ecom: physical products carry low margins. Software "has zero cost for distribution", so "the only cost is marketing" and it is almost pure profit.
- He says an app can start "from your bedroom", especially with AI and vibe coding, and that "if you prompt it well, you can create a multi-million dollar app."
- Two things changed since he started: building is far easier, and the zero-to-100k playbook is now widely known. When he began, "you figure it out yourself"; now founders share strategies openly online.
- Benchmarks he cites: Quitter did $30k in its first month. Kai did $250k. Cal AI went from $50k in month two to $100k in month three and then to half a million. Flo does about $10 million a month. Before these, he says, nobody had shown what was possible in consumer apps.
- His own failures came first. At 17 he tried to raise $100 million pre-seed for an Instagram/Facebook/Twitter-style social platform and "failed brutally". He then built Rich AI, which also failed, before Quitter.

chunks.heading: How he built the belief that a million a month was possible
chunks.text:
- His vision did not start as "two or three million a month". It came from a friend (Zach Yadegari of Cal AI) proving the path first.
- He snuck into a hotel in Fontainebleau, Miami while broke and met Zach, who was making about $1k a month from consumer apps. Months later Zach said Cal AI would hit 50k in a month, and it did.
- Alex started building his own app once peers were around $200k a month.
- His rule: "Whatever Zach achieved, I know I could do." Seeing a peer reach a number makes it a template rather than a fantasy.
- Seeing a peer win without you also drives him. He describes imagining that heartbreak ("I could have done it myself but I didn't") as the strongest motivation, and says something in the app world recently gave him that feeling "in a positive way".

chunks.heading: Keep the big picture, but work from the first sale
chunks.text:
- Alex says to know how big the idea can get. A product that's perfect for one person won't necessarily get millions to use it, so start with "a big idea, high pain point".
- He warns against fixating on "millions a month" while you have $10 in revenue, because it kills motivation.
- His scaling sequence: get the first sale, then 10, then 100, then 1,000. "If you make money in one channel, if you did 100x the output, could you make 100x more?"
- On his own goals, he treats milestones as stepping stones: $500k a month is revenue, not profit, and not personal income, so he doesn't put achievements "on a pedestal".

chunks.heading: Scaling paid ads: speed
chunks.text:
- Quitter has run around $500k a month on Twitter ads since roughly April or May. As of January 2026 he calls that too slow ("I've been way too slow stabbing for Twitter") and is ramping up.
- The plan: increase daily ad spend by 20% a day. He expected about $1 million a month within a week and about $2 million a month the week after.
- He says he wants "a whole new focus on speed and scaling" and admits the company missed that for a while.
- He says one day in Miami helped him close roughly $1.1 million of investment and "completely flip the trajectory" of Quitter, and that the pace of the Miami environment was a big part of it.

chunks.heading: Drive over curiosity
chunks.text:
- Alex and Zach concluded they succeeded because they're interested in the world: "The more you learn, the more you understand, the more you know what to do next."
- Alex then says drive matters more than curiosity. You can sit in his Discord, learn how to scale an app from zero to a million and recite it, but "if you don't have the drive to actually figure it out and do it yourself, you're not going to make it."
- Drive creates interest: even if the interest wasn't there originally, drive gave him the interest to figure things out.
- He credits massive self-belief: "I don't understand why I would not believe to the max and put all the work in and figure it out."
- Tools such as vibe coding make building easier, but he believes the determined people "will figure it out regardless of circumstances". His blunt view is that "you're either a killer or you're not."
- If he hadn't succeeded with Quitter, he says he'd "have done something else" and would never have stopped until he made it.

chunks.heading: Reacting to other people's success
chunks.text:
- Asked about people discouraged by seeing flexing on social media, Alex says he finds that reaction unnatural and offers a reframe: treat the money flowing through the ecosystem as proof, and ask "how can I do the same thing?"
- He describes seeing a multimillion-dollar plane overhead and thinking there's a whole other world of business to learn, instead of being ignorant of it.
- He notes that the app space lets founders show revenue that's publicly verifiable, which builds trust.

chunks.heading: Exit plan and next moves
chunks.text:
- His stated plan is to sell Quitter for around $100 million within roughly four to twelve months. He calls it "totally realistic".
- After that he plans to go into music next, citing Drake, Kanye and Rihanna: the power of attention and image is valuable, and another tech company would make him "too much of a nerd tech guy".
- Long term he wants to enter UK politics, because he believes UK leaders are not real business people and he wants to be a billionaire with that power.
- He says business skills don't decay, so he could return to real business later.

chunks.heading: Environment matters: Miami vs London
chunks.text:
- Alex got a $10 million Miami house for YouTube content, was evicted a few months later for throwing too many parties, and moved back to London to be near friends and family.
- After two months in London he returned to Miami, closed the roughly $1.1 million investment on day one, and found he wanted to stay.
- His reasons: Miami moves faster, has "billions of dollars of people" around, and has far more entrepreneurial peers. London has few entrepreneurial friends and bad weather.
- His rule for his 20s: surround yourself with people smarter and more successful rather than being "the best one in the city", and don't commit a year to a place that won't help you grow the most. He previously moved to the US on an O-1 visa for this reason.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A live Q&A with the Quitter founders on scaling a consumer app past influencer marketing. Alex covers pricing for volume, validating ideas via competitor revenue, shipping fast with AI, retention through community, and moving from organic to paid ads as revenue grows.

chunks.heading: Pricing and the paywall: low entry price, volume over per-user revenue
chunks.text:
- Quitter's app (a porn-quitting app) moved off its original price of $12.99 a month and $45 a year, where most revenue came from the yearly plan. The new price is $6.99 a week and $29.99 a year.
- The point of the change was to lower the barrier to join. Alex says (credited to Blake Anderson) "it's not about how much you can make per paying user, it's about the volume of users you can get to pay for a smaller amount", because that produces more total revenue.
- Payments run through Superwall, which integrates with Apple Pay.
- Quitter has no free trial, except an offer shown to people who are uninstalling the app. Alex's reasons:
  - The business is predictable: a given number of downloads converts to a known number of sales and revenue, which is reinvested into marketing. Free trials add uncertainty that would disrupt that, especially in November, their biggest month.
  - "When something's free people act like it's free." Retention and activity go up when people pay, because they have high intent to use the app and join the community.
  - They would rather lose some users and have the rest pay than give the app away and try to convert later.
- About 85% of users do not convert on the initial paywall. Alex is collecting emails so that discounts can be pushed to that 85%, with the hope that 10-20% of them convert. He calls it a numbers game and a way to "squeeze as much juice" out of every download.
- In the onboarding flow the app asks for a review. Only about 1% do it, but at 20,000 downloads that is about 200 reviews. It also asks again while people are using the app.

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing: how Alex structures deals and pays
chunks.text:
- Standard deal: a retainer of about $1,000 a month for one video a week (four a month), plus a minimum view count and video count per month. Alex says "the key is volume".
- Alex was paying about $1 per thousand views early on and calls that a very good deal. It has since moved to roughly $2-3 per thousand, and in general it comes out between $1 and $5. They are about to test paying $1-2 per thousand views directly.
- Because deals have minimum videos and views, he can estimate ROI: if 100,000 views bring in X in revenue, then multiplying by four months shows what the retainer is worth. Contracts can be structured to test a creator first.
- Not every thousand views is worth the same:
  - A video with 20-40k views earned about $2,000 (he also cites a roughly 40,000-view video earning about $2,000 and a 20-30k one making "two free grand" in the speech).
  - A 1 million view video earned about $200.
- Takeaway: find out who watches the creator and whether they are your target market. If so, pay for engagement even at 20,000 views a video, and he would pay more for a highly engaged creator than for a viral one with little engagement.
- How he evaluates creators: he looks for consistent views (5-10k, 10-20k, 30-50k per video with some hits near 100k) rather than follower count. A creator with a million followers who gets 20,000 views will still ask for a lot of money. He then reads the comments to see whether people ask about solutions to the problem the app solves, and he says he "eyeballs" engagement rather than using a fixed metric.
- Negotiation: be honest about budget ("my budget is only $2,000, can we do a few trial videos"). He learned from Ridge Wallet that when someone asks for a figure like $6,000 it is usually what they want. Talk to creators on a call, and expect to DM about 100 influencers to get one response.
- Spread the budget: do not put all eggs in one basket. With a couple of thousand dollars, deploy about $500 a month across four creators for three to four videos each, and use different creators with different creatives.
- Creative control: give creators a structure but let them stay in their own style. Pushing something inorganic to their audience does not work, and Alex says they made that mistake before. Make sure the app is pushed in the call to action, subtly.
- Tracking: they give creators codes and also line up post times against when sales arrive. Codes only capture some sales, so they use them mostly to see where traffic comes from, and pay creators a flat $3 per code use in some arrangements so that not every user is paid for.
- A creator's audience matters more than the CTA. Alex says a Horsey-style creator's video converted well with a subtle CTA because of that creator's engaged, dark-humor audience, not because of the call to action.
- Where Alex is moving next: shifting from "draining" a creator's existing audience toward viral content that reaches a wider audience, with deals that incentivize creators to post viral material.
- Outreach tips: go through TikTok, Instagram, emails, even LinkedIn if needed. Be respectful but follow up, since many people are busy and a bump often gets a reply.

chunks.heading: First users, validation and finding an idea
chunks.text:
- Alex got his first users from Reddit and Twitter organic posting. He made $2,000 from Reddit before being banned, and says the workaround is making other accounts. This is for the early stage without money.
- Timeline: 20,000 downloads in a month, with paying customers within about two weeks.
- How they chose the idea: both founders arrived separately at porn addiction. Alex says the top app in the category made about $100K a month, with only about 10,000 downloads, and "there's millions of men struggling with this". Knowing a competitor made that revenue gave him confidence it was a business.
- Tool: Sensor Tower (sensortower.com) to see competitor revenue and market size. Alex notes it is an estimate and that it can run about half of the real figure, but it is a good reference.
- Alex's advice for choosing an idea: use Sensor Tower to find categories where apps make millions, copy the winners (he mentions sleep apps), and win on distribution. Copying a proven idea "significantly reduces your risk".
- A complementary view from his co-founder: validate by seeing competitors making money, then out-distribute them.
- Pre-launch demand: you can run ads on several ideas to see which gets the most sign-ups, but Alex would rather trust his gut and build, because you learn more by building. A friend used ManyChat so people DM'd for access and got on a waitlist, and Alex says that is fine if it makes the founder feel more secure.

chunks.heading: Building the product: speed, quality bar and tech
chunks.text:
- Alex builds in SwiftUI. He skips Android because it makes around 20% of what Apple's platform does in revenue.
- He leans on AI heavily: "you can build any app of your dreams in two, three days". Most of the Quitter app, including the hard parts like communities, was built with AI. Method: tell it what you want, paste the code, run it, and iterate with prompts until it matches what you picture. He also expects Xcode to add full AI app creation.
- Backend: Firebase for databases and Heroku for hosting, with payment security handled by Apple and platform providers rather than custom work.
- Quality bar: "don't ship something that you wouldn't use yourself." If you would not pay for it, it is a bad product. He is a perfectionist and says that trait stopped him from shipping. His advice is to spend an extra week making it a bit better, then push, and that someone will pay for anything you put out.
- Co-founder Connor adds: "great distribution with an average app beats a great app with average distribution," as long as the app solves the problem. Quitter went three months without its core content-blocking feature working and still reached almost $100,000 in revenue.
- Why mobile over web: everyone has a phone and consumers spend more on apps because payment is one tap.
- Content blocking plan: use Apple's Screen Time adult-content block setting, which the app can override, plus a desktop version later.
- Development vs marketing: Alex says development is harder to learn, but he thinks you need both, since marketing does not work with weak product or pricing.

chunks.heading: Community as a moat and retention driver
chunks.text:
- The Telegram community existed from the start. Alex did nothing special to make it engaging, people simply asked questions and talked, and it grew slowly. That showed how valuable it was and led to a forum in the app, then moderators.
- He considers community "the best thing for retention": subscribers lean on it when they are struggling, so it is worth paying for.
- It is also a moat. Alex says you cannot "just rip off Quitter and make money because we have a community."
- Gamification plus community: once people build momentum they usually keep it.

chunks.heading: Scaling beyond influencers
chunks.text:
