- Alex and Connor are building systems to automate what is currently manual (DM the creator, sign a contract, watch results) into a repeatable formula that reaches many more creators.
- Plan by stage, from a document Alex shared: $0-10K a month is basic ASO plus organic posts; at $1M-$5M-$10M a month it is mostly paid ads, because ads let you allocate budget and force content at scale without the DM bottleneck. Master one stage before moving to the next.
- Paid ads: Meta ads launching that day (the ad was approved as he spoke). Targeting is men 20-28, US-based, health and fitness, with a broad pixel finding the audience, and creatives including street interviews, app demos and a 28-day challenge. Tracking uses the Facebook SDK in the app.
- Why Meta even if worse than influencers: influencers might return 10x on some deals, but Meta gives a consistent 2-3x that can be scaled by adding budget. He mentions that a competitor reportedly scales to $2,500 a day, which suggests it works.
- Tests coming: clipping content (for example from self-help and podcast figures talking about why porn is bad) to push volume; he also likes the idea of a dedicated Twitter-style page and notes viral videos can sometimes be reposted on a new account for similar results, which he hasn't validated himself.
- The ASO effect: more organic and external traffic raises app store rank. Searching "quit porn" puts Quitter around third and they are aiming for first.

chunks.heading: Co-founders, equity and personal brand
chunks.text:
- Finding a co-founder: Y Combinator co-founder matching, or Twitter (messaging people in Blake Anderson's comments). Alex says you must be able to code, or you are "that guy that can't code". Co-founder Connor brought money to fund the first influencers, had a knack for sales and negotiation, and complements Alex's skills.
- Influencers and equity: Alex warns about giving equity to influencers. A friend, Zack, gave an influencer equity, later tried to terminate the contract, and is now being taken to court after the company grew. Alex's view is to pay a small fee and test, not give equity. Connor adds that if you do give equity, use a vesting cliff tied to conditions such as staying a year and delivering specific work.
- Personal brand: Alex thinks now is a "gold rush" and that those who build a personal brand and share information before the space saturates will last. He values it more long term than making money from a single app.
- Selling to wealthy parents (advice given to a student building tools for high school competitions): sell the outcome, such as getting into an Ivy League, rather than a higher score, and learn how existing tutors acquire clients. Alex's blunt view is that if the goal is money, copy proven categories rather than invent a niche.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A chaotic vlog of the Soar team spending a big marketing budget on stunts in San Francisco: branded cars, hackathon sponsorships, QR flight credits and press-bait tweets. The useful ideas are building mind share through memorable stunts, documenting it, and pairing hype with a fast product.

chunks.heading: Soar's guerrilla launch: stunts, flight credits and "mind share" in San Francisco
chunks.text:
Alex's team (Soar, a flight-booking platform) set a goal of getting 100,000 San Franciscans to use the product. Alex describes the setup as "a million dollars to spend on marketing", with investors adding more money.

- The tactics are loud and physical: a Cybertruck, a Lamborghini, a cheap 1980 Volvo, a TV truck driving around the city, planes, billboards, hackathon sponsorships, paper planes thrown from a roof, and a treasure hunt with a million-dollar prize.
- Everyone in SF "works all day". The team wants to "bring some life to the city" and get everyone taking photos and knowing what Soar is.
- The deliberately meme-y "vault of investor money" branding is meant to make some people mad. The logic: if people mock it and it works, "we're right".
- Reported traction: the team says it is "nearing a million dollars in flights booked" about 2 months after launch, and hit a record day of roughly 28K in booking volume.
- Booking counts rose daily: 41, then 42, then 47 bookings in a day, including 8 bookings in one minute.

chunks.heading: Mind share first, then convert with a good product
chunks.text:
Alex lays out the core logic: do stunts so everyone in the city knows the brand, and some will try it when they need a flight.

- "Anyone needs to book a flight might try us. They try us and they like us, they'll stay." He frames the goal as positive ROI while having fun.
- He argues that "you get enough eyes on the brand, you have a good product, like that's all that really matters." Location (San Francisco vs Miami) doesn't matter.
- The market is big: Alex pitches flight booking as roughly "a trillion a year", with incumbents (Skyscanner, Google Flights, booking.com) that are "old companies" and no "life" in the category.
- Product proof points used in pitches: booking in about 13 seconds, saved details, auto check-in, agent booking for airlines without a booking API, and iMessage/text booking. The team also pitches "book flights faster than this car" as an exaggerated hook.
- Refund protection is sold as a $17 add-on that makes a flight fully refundable for any reason until departure. Soar offers it itself, not through the airline.
- Early traction came from Twitter: Alex says the first week got about 2 million views.

chunks.heading: QR-code flight credits and gamified giveaways
chunks.text:
Offline distribution is built on cheap, trackable incentives that get strangers to try the product.

- The team handed out roughly 200-300 QR codes outside YC Startup School, each giving a $25 discount. Alex estimates the stack is "easily like 3K worth of flight credits" for the month.
- A blackjack game is played with passers-by: win and get $25 in credit, lose and "you lose nothing. There's no risk here." It turns a flyer handoff into a conversation and a demo.
- In conversations, the team demos booking on the spot and pitches against pain points people mention (for example, a customer who lost most of a flight's cost despite travel insurance).
- A tweet offering $250 in flight credit to anyone who brings a girl to the party was funny enough that a news outlet (Business Insider Australia) wanted to cover it. Alex's plan is to post the coverage on Twitter and get people to repost or quote-tweet it.
- His summary of the approach: "we just got to keep doing stuff like this, literally."

chunks.heading: Branded car and wearable assets for events
chunks.text:
The 1980 Volvo and merch are used as rolling billboards.

- The Volvo cost about $2,000, is unregistered and was bought for fun and visibility ("You going to see why I like shitboxes?"). Alex says plates from another car are used to drive it.
- New designs on the cars and apparel (a faded gradient matching the app's UI "clouds") mean "we can now go into hackathons or events and they'll see the logo and be like, 'Oh [expletive] you're the Soar guys.'"
- He considers chalk spray paint as a cheap further creative touch.
- The team keeps a rule of picking up stunt ideas from other founders. A person who runs crazy stunts like "Hollyweed" approached them to get involved.

chunks.heading: Content as a distribution channel
chunks.text:
The whole campaign is filmed as a vlog series, and the content itself is part of the marketing.

- Alex's reasoning: someone interested in startups who watches the vlogs will see the brand, try it, follow along, and tell friends.
- He sells the series on two things: entertainment ("sit back, chill with your boys") and learning ("you'll learn a lot if you stay with us").

chunks.heading: Lessons from the Airbnb party incident
chunks.text:
The team's public party invite got them removed from their rental, which shows the risk of public stunts.

- A tweet linking an open party at their Airbnb was spotted by Airbnb, which told the host the group could not stay (policy against parties). Alex says they had AI-generated the first listing image, and the team had not actually thrown the party at that house.
- They were asked to leave within a day and replaced the rental with a house in Danville with a hot tub, booked at what Alex called "8,000 euros".
- Alex's take: record bookings kept coming ("we've been breaking our record every day") even while housing was in chaos, so the stunt cost was acceptable. Public links can create real operational problems, though.

chunks.heading: Hiring and team signals
chunks.text:
The team picks up growth talent by watching who shows up.

- A candidate for head of growth said he scaled a previous company to a couple hundred thousand and pitched himself on hunger: he flew in and showed up when "nothing was guaranteed".
- Alex jokes that they "did just fire our head of growth. Wasn't good enough."
- The team found the candidate's location using an AI image search of a tweet photo, and found phone numbers through paid data tools ($5 to $60), which they treated as a sign of resourcefulness.
- Soar's team has one developer on the back end, building the agent booking and auto check-in.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The App Mafia founders (RizzGPT, UMax, Cali, Quitter, about $50M combined revenue) explain why AI plus easy builds plus influencer marketing created a new consumer app wave. They also cover lean teams, high-agency hiring and when a personal brand is worth it. The transcript has no speaker labels, so attribution to Alex is best-effort.

chunks.heading: Alex's path into apps and the Riz GPT launch
chunks.text:
- Alex's first app, Peer Pressure, failed. He then saw consumer utility apps working and got serious about the space after a friend sent him a podcast featuring Blake Anderson and Omar.
- He was at buildspace season 5 in San Francisco. He had met Zach-side collaborator Connor eight months earlier through YC co-founder matching, when Connor was looking for a developer. Connor pitched an app to help men quit porn. Alex had already built it the week before, and Connor took on marketing. That became Quitter.
- Alex's reasoning for Riz GPT: people should be packaging ChatGPT into apps, and more and more people consume on phones rather than laptops. His plan was to build a product and market it on social media.
- He picked the most obvious idea: an AI dating assistant for guys who don't know how to talk to girls. The user uploads a screenshot and the app tells them what to say.
- He expected $10-20K a month, "enough for me to live" while he built other businesses. It did 80,000 MRR within 3 days of launch.
- The launch channel was influencer marketing with "underground niche, underpriced creators" who had a "super cult-like following." This was the very start of the AI app wave, when mobile apps were mostly social tools (NGL, TBH, Gas, Instagram wrapped).

chunks.heading: Why consumer apps took off now: three macro trends
chunks.text:
Alex lays out three shifts, and says every new player in this space uses at least two, usually all three:

1. **New technology.** From the launch of the App Store until the release of ChatGPT in 2022-2023, there were no big technology shifts. Most big players were founded in the early 2010s (My Fitness Pal, Headspace, Calm) and kept winning. LLMs let you embed real functionality into a single-player product.
2. **Building is easier.** You used to need to hire developers, raise capital, or be highly skilled. Now you can code with LLMs, and database providers like Supabase are far easier to use.
3. **Dropshipping-style marketing.** It is very easy to get a product in front of people through influencers.

chunks.heading: Why influencer marketing works for apps
chunks.text:
- The group sees influencer marketing as still working for apps, where some ecommerce founders say it is dead for physical products.
- Alex's explanation is novelty: shorts or gym clothes will "never be as novel as some like crazy new AI tech." A post about a new app can go more viral than the creator's average post.
- Emotional pain points also help. With Quitter, quitting porn is a strong emotional pain for men, and a community that helps them is what they need. The influencer or meme is only the vehicle.
- On saturation: Alex says the low-hanging AI app ideas have been captured, but novel ideas still have room. He notes that most influencer promos are for physical products, not apps, so apps are not what is crowding influencers.
- Deal structure is what makes it profitable. The group's contracts are an in-between of flat fee and incentive-based, with terms built to ensure a certain number of views. He also points out that an ecommerce brand switched to the Cali-style strategy of paying influencers with big followings instead of micro accounts where "one out of 10 videos would blow up."

chunks.heading: Low-effort, high-margin apps
chunks.text:
- At the time of recording, Riz GPT does about $4M a year and UMAX about $4M a year, with Cali just under $40M (about $45M across the three). With Quitter at about $6M, the group is just over $50M in annual revenue.
- Alex's point: "if you build a good product, you don't have to maintain it. The code continues to provide the service on its own, and if you have the marketing system set up correctly, it'll just continue printing."
- Those apps run at over 50% profit margins. Each of UMAX and Riz GPT has only one full-time employee, a social media manager, plus a VA.
- Revenue on these apps is flat rather than churning, and the products are still being sold mostly to new users through ongoing downloads. Plans are weekly and other tiers.

chunks.heading: Monetizing the community without selling out the business
chunks.text:
- App Mafia runs a free 14-hour course for people new to the space, and a paid "Insiders" community with an introductory call, weekly office hours, coaches and a network of successful founders.
- The reasoning: they get 100+ inbound requests a day for advice, and the paid community is how they decide who gets time. One member went from about 10K MRR to over 80K MRR.
- All the cash goes back into the community or operations (videographers, editors, clippers), not out as personal income.
- Strategic upside: learning what founders need and who succeeds helps if they later build a fund. Their personal brands grow, which they can use for hiring and for future businesses.
- Alex frames the content chapter as a personal-brand phase, not his whole life, running alongside his apps.

chunks.heading: Personal brand: when it helps and when it doesn't
chunks.text:
- Alex argues against a one-size-fits-all rule. A personal brand has upsides (attention, DMs, options, hiring, influencing views) and costs (privacy, time).
- If you are building deep tech or B2B SaaS where distribution does not depend on social media, "posting little short-form skits isn't going to do anything for your business," and effort should be spent carefully.
- He still sees "a lot of opportunity and alpha" in building one, because eyes on your work give you options and let you "nudge the world."
- Long-term ambition: be the "Mr. Beast of entrepreneurship," giving people business entertainment instead of mindless entertainment.

chunks.heading: Advice for starting from zero
chunks.text:
- Alex's own view, which he returns to as the closing advice: study and reverse-engineer successful products. He says the internet is "open sourced": you can see a competitor's App Store screenshots, logo, marketing and product and realise "I could probably do that too."
- Revenue as proof: "it only takes $1 revenue to give you the self-belief to keep pushing higher." He promised himself that after the first $10 sale he could reach 100, then 1,000. The first month hit 30K.
- Persistence: a founder should keep launching until one works.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex argues the hardest part of launching anything (apps, music, art) is getting people to care, not making it. He says image and inspiration drive attention, and marketing should centre the user's better future rather than "download my app." Persistence through early indifference is key.

chunks.heading: Why getting people to care is the hardest part of marketing
chunks.text:
- Alex says getting people to care is "pretty much the hardest thing you have to do as a person."
- Building something you love (art, an album, an app) guarantees nothing. He describes releasing a piece he was sure would "take over the world" and getting nothing.
- Everyone has their own life going on. "Why would they care about you and what you've released? Doesn't matter if it's good."
- Thought experiment: release Drake's or Kanye's exact discography, same albums and covers. Without an audience, "go find some listeners." Distribution and attention are the problem, not the quality of the work.
- He thinks this is what kills most people's ambitions. Friends who launched apps inspired by his and Chris's started with strong self-belief, got no traction, then doubted themselves ("am I delusional?") and gave up.
- His advice: expect to be "humbled very, very hard" when the world doesn't care on day one, then "stay persistent, stay consistent."

chunks.heading: Image and persona as a way to get people to care (music example)
chunks.text:
- For music, Alex says caring starts with your image and who you are as a person, not just the songs.
- SD Kid: his covered face leaves people's minds to "fill in the blanks" and assume he's cool. Alex argues that unmasked, the same music might not hit the same way.
- Drake: "If Drake was a loser, no one would listen to Drake." The artist's lifestyle and persona make people sing the music.
- Joji: he was Filthy Frank, a big YouTube creator in a pink suit, but wanted to make sad music. Alex says that character couldn't credibly do it, so he dropped it and became someone new, and people can now sing his music "unironically."
- Alex applies this to himself: he decided not to tie his name too closely to software or data ("I can't be too nerdy"), because it would hurt his image and the audience he wants for music.
- His intended persona: a young guy in London making exceptional music, dresses well, drives a nice car, has on-point Instagram captions, and a way of life that is "amazing to follow."
- Takeaway: "Getting people to care sometimes is as simple as inspiring them."

chunks.heading: Put the user first in every piece of marketing (apps)
chunks.text:
- Don't go on Reddit and say "I just released this app, download it." Alex says "that's not how you get people to care."
- In every piece of marketing, put the user first and show them their life could be incredible if they used the app. "People care mostly about themselves."
- Example with his app Reset, addressed to a viewer named Andrew: "You can become the best version of yourself. I know you're not in the place you want to be right now, but you can be if you try Reset."
- The reader then thinks about being healthy, happy and stronger, and tries it "because it's for me."
- The switch: "Instead of being like 'download my app,' you're like 'transform your life.' These are very different things."

chunks.heading: Don't copy content you don't believe in
chunks.text:
- Alex criticises posting TikTok content you don't believe in and are only copying because it works. He addresses this to Lucas Plumbridge and Chris, who worked on the Discover app.
- He grants "there is some element of truth" in copying what works, but says you must "always put yourself first."
- Questions he suggests asking: What do you believe the world needs? What is it missing? How can you improve?
- His claim: if you get that right, "everything else should follow."

chunks.heading: Inspire to sell
chunks.text:
- Core rule: always ask "how do I make the other person inspired?"
- "If you can inspire someone, you can sell to them," whether the product is an app, your music or your modelling.
- Marketing your own products yourself is, in his words, the hardest thing you have to do. Persistence matters because people "will figure out in due time."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex reflects on 2025 at Quitter Aid: $4.2M revenue but far less cash because of loose spending, and a year of underinvesting in Meta ads while paying underperforming influencers. He also covers posting before it's perfect and mindset.

chunks.heading: Mistakes are information, not failure
chunks.text:
- Alex says mistakes happen because "you don't understand what you're doing well enough, because if you did, you would just do it the right way."
- Since it's everyone's first time living, he treats messing up as inevitable.
- His rule: "the aim of the game really is just to not make the same mistake twice." Ask why you messed up, then be better next time.

chunks.heading: Be financially responsible: run the real numbers
chunks.text:
- Quitter Aid (his app business) did $4.2 million in revenue in 2025, but Alex says the bank account "definitely isn't that number."
- Cause: "we just spent way too much money on dumb [stuff]." Generating hundreds of thousands of dollars a month made him feel invincible, especially with no prior business success.
- His worked example, at about $7,000/day of proceeds (revenue after Apple's cut):
  - minus about $3,500/day of ad spend
  - minus monthly team overheads divided by 30
  - minus Apple's cut and any random spending
  - minus fancy dinners and similar
  - Result: nothing left.
- Proceeds are now about $15,000/day, versus about $7,000/day back when the spending was reckless.
- Advice: "be smart, take it easy, take it slow, and be clinical." Run the math properly and don't run it in your favor. Don't tell yourself "I'm making X a month, I can do whatever I want"; know where you actually are.

chunks.heading: Don't be afraid to post
chunks.text:
- Alex admits he held back posting unless it was perfect, "at the SL standard," to avoid critique.
- His realization: "The world just forgets you." He cites Liam Payne, once globally recognized, now rarely discussed.
- People follow you for a reason. If you stop posting they don't really notice or care, because they have other accounts to consume.
- His conclusion: "If you feel like you have something to bring to the world, bring it to the world. Don't hold back."

chunks.heading: Believe you're meant to be great
chunks.text:
- Alex's claim: if you think you're going to be great, you're already more than halfway there.
- He backs his own confidence with specific skills: sales, branding, marketing, product and pricing, plus "killer instincts." He says people who think this way "are supposed to be great."
- Don't put money or success on a pedestal. Those who want it most and put in the most work get it.
- Framing: the law of cause and effect. "Everything you have in your life right now is a result of what you've put in." If you're unhappy, it's because you avoided the work, so "go hustle and get it."

chunks.heading: Accept what isn't meant to be
chunks.text:
- Alex says "everything happens for a reason and what will be will be."
- In 2025 he put too much pressure on things that didn't work out and got frustrated over things that "wasn't supposed to be anyway."
- Two reactions are available: get upset and frustrated, or accept that this isn't in your story. If it isn't supposed to be, it isn't.

chunks.heading: Focus on what really matters: put the budget where it works
chunks.text:
- Quitter Aid spent about $100K a month on Meta ads from February 2025 and did not increase the budget for the rest of the year.
- The team also paid influencers who weren't performing, because that was the game everyone else on Twitter was playing. Alex says there was no self-realization about whether it was right for the business, and it wasn't.
- On returning to the company, he pushed to raise the Meta budget and drop influencer pay into Meta.
- Result: proceeds of about $15,000/day, roughly $18,000-$20,000 gross revenue per day. He says it was "as simple as just doubling the budget on Meta" and that they should have done it ages ago.
- Next steps he names: keep raising ad budget, improve creatives, and diversify into SEO and Google search ads. The goal is reaching "2, 3, 4 million" months.
- Feeling at a standstill with Quitter Aid is part of why he started his other app, Reset: he wanted to move faster.

chunks.heading: Relationships: don't ignore red flags
chunks.text:
- Alex met his ex in December 2024 and knew almost immediately it was "kind of pointless," with many red flags.
- He kept the relationship going out of comfort. Messages from February 2025 that he found later were clearly "toxic," yet it lasted until December.
- The reasons he didn't like her at the start were the same reasons he broke up with her at the end.
- His view: relationships "affect every aspect of your life" and become a cornerstone, so be intentional and careful. Act when you know instead of pushing it off.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A vlog from inside a 20-year-old founder's flight-booking startup during a heavy marketing push. Alex explains positioning against commoditized airlines, the one-tap Tesla analogy, spending investment money on attention stunts, and a fraud problem that came with sudden growth. The creator-sponsorship playbook is mostly described by his YouTube head, Nathan.

chunks.heading: Positioning: attacking a commoditized, confusing flight-booking market
chunks.text:
- Alex's pitch for Saw (spelled "Sore" in the transcript) is "the best way to book flights": "[ __ ] Google Flights. [ __ ] Sky Scanner. Join the future. Book in one click."
- Extras he lists: auto check-in and iMessage flight updates.
- He is 20 and the founder. He describes his own role as co-founder: hiring, coming up with new ideas, and "doing the growth."
- His diagnosis of the category:
  - "No one's innovated. Everyone's too scared to because the margins on flights, they're very low. They're commoditized."
  - Airline companies "make money by confusing you with the upsells, the multiple pages." Flights themselves "will generate nothing."
- His bet is to win on experience even at lower margin: "even if we make less money, we can still be the best. And like that that is like very powerful."

chunks.heading: Business model idea: simple product first, monetize bags, seats and later hotels
chunks.text:
- Alex's planned revenue is a small fee on add-ons: "if we charge like a small fee on bags and seats and then maybe we get into hotels, I think we'll be fine."
- The product promise is one tap: find the flight, book, enter code, done. He contrasts it with the old internet's "multiple pages of [ __ ]."
- He compares Saw to Tesla's direct online car sales: Tesla cut the clicks needed to buy a car online and removed the upsell-heavy flow, and he says "what Tesla did to the auto industry is kind of like what we're doing."
- The ambition he states: "I want 100 million people using it." He says he "really see[s] that being a reality."

chunks.heading: Attention-grabbing branding: spending investment money on a car
chunks.text:
- Alex owns a branded Saw car, bought partly with raised money: "we raised some money. We spent some investment money on it. And hey, look, it gets the attention. So, job well done."
- He treats it as an attention play and judges it by the attention it gets, with no ROI figure given.
- His stated personal goal is "just be the best. Be the biggest."

chunks.heading: Fraud problem: stolen cards and VOIP numbers booking expensive flights
chunks.text:
- Alex describes a fraud wave that first hit in June and came back. It comes from people in Accra, Ghana, who he thinks are using stolen credit cards.
- The signals he sees in the orders:
  - Fake VOIP phone numbers, so the customer has no iMessage.
  - High-ticket flights, such as $1.2K and $3.3K.
  - A stream of disputes in Stripe that Saw is losing: "lost, lost, lost, lost, lost."
- Why a simple country ban won't work: "someone's actually going to have a real flight from there and that's not good."
- His candidate fix is to compare the name on the card with the name on the flight and ban on a mismatch.
- The flaw he sees in that rule is personal assistants who legitimately book flights for other people, so banning that whole group isn't sustainable. He leaves it unresolved ("I need to figure this out").
- Volume check: he counted six flights in one hour and extrapolated to about 120 flights a day.
- He also wants a notification every time a Saw user is in the air.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Slater vlogs a typical CEO day at his app Quitter: checking ad spend and revenue, managing the team, and hiring creatives and a CPO. He explains why Meta ad creative is the biggest lever, why equity and exits matter more than monthly cash, and what he learned from taking sole leadership.

chunks.heading: Running Quitter as a CEO: the day-to-day job is managing people, not doing the work
chunks.text:
- Alex took back sole CEO status from a co-founder split. He says two leaders each owning "50% of responsibilities" left everyone confused and nobody overseeing the whole. As sole leader he talks to every employee daily, knows what is going on and what to hire for.
- He says the result was record months in January and February, with March on track to be bigger than both.
- His morning routine: catch up with the team on Slack, keep everyone on Rome (a virtual office tool), check Meta ad spend, and check the day's proceeds.
- Most of the CEO job is calling the full-time employees he pays to execute and checking they are doing a good job. He says this means a lot of waiting around, and he always finds something else to do, especially on weekends when others are off.
- He works at lunch too, reviewing a Loom-video application to join the team. His view: "the amount of care that you have for something reflects in the outcomes."

chunks.heading: Meta ads: creative is the lever, and more angles expand the addressable market
chunks.text:
- Alex says Meta targets automatically from the creative, like the Reels algorithm. A motivation video gets shown to people with motivation content on their feeds.
- He believes most specific Meta ad settings "don't really matter" now. It is all about creative.
- Lesson he says he learned: the company needs more angles and different styles of creator, because that expands the audience. Quitter had sold well to young people who want to quit. Untapped groups he names: Muslims, Christians, gym bros and people who want high testosterone. To reach them, change the creative and Meta will show it to those people.
- He calls hiring a creative team Quitter's top focus.
- Revenue dips when Meta Ads has outages. On one such day he cites about 15.5k in proceeds, which he calls "all right" rather than great, blaming Meta showing ads to the wrong people.
- His three levers: more differently styled creatives, more money into the system, and fixing attribution. He says "we'll be taking over" if all three happen.

chunks.heading: Building the creative team at scale
chunks.text:
- A Tribe campaign has roughly 300 creators who post for Quitter, producing about 1.3k creatives a month in different styles. Alex says he believes the figure is about 300 people.
- He is also trying to hire a creative director who can script and produce very high production videos at scale, with captions and editing, like Get Brick and other e-commerce brands. He thinks Quitter should try the same.

chunks.heading: Hiring a Chief Product Officer to squeeze more from the product
chunks.text:
- Alex is hunting for a CPO through a head hunter named Ken, at about 25K a month. His reasoning: "What else am I going to do with the 25K a month? Throw it in the profit tank?"
- His ideal candidate has worked at big companies like Duolingo and knows high-level product changes that raise revenue, ARPU, LTV and customer satisfaction.
- Areas he wants them to obsess over: retention improvements within the community, and onboarding.
- SEO idea: rank the community for searches like "I'm struggling with porn, my wife hates me", the way Reddit does, so Quitter becomes a social platform.
- He argues that as spend and downloads grow, small percentage improvements matter a lot more.

chunks.heading: Why he reinvests: equity and exits beat cash
chunks.text:
- He points to Cal AI being acquired by MyFitnessPal, with the announcement tweet getting 7 million views, as a blueprint for Quitter.
- His view: apps can claim half a million or 5 million a month, but take-home after marketing spend is modest. The real prize is the exit from "building a brand legacy and tens of millions of downloads", which he calls the magnum opus of the app space. "It isn't really cash, it's the big exits, the equity value."
- So he is ramping up: "We need to spend way more money and we need to go forward faster. Speed, speed, speed." He says he expects two, three, four million dollar months soon.
- Small dividends (he mentions 10K) "don't really matter much". The real money is in equity and long-term profit.

chunks.heading: First real profit and cash management
chunks.text:
- On the day filmed, Apple's payout landed and he describes it as the first time the company had real gross profit it could retain without reinvesting. He says the company owes nearly nobody, and that for many months it did not turn a profit.
- He says about 300K more was still on the way and that profit was around 600K gross after debts were paid.
- He puts ad spend on a credit card and says he hit his card limit, with a balance of about 321k, so he paid it down as soon as the payout arrived.
- His point on money and time: a parking ticket only hurts because of the time it takes to earn the fine back. When touching a lot of money a month, you can absorb small costs like that without guilt.

chunks.heading: Focus versus lifestyle
chunks.text:
- He says he does not vlog often because most days are repetitive desk work.
- His claim: "You can't have a super exciting life and also make an insane amount of progress. You need to pick one or the other."
- He says he balances this well but is "nowhere near the place I want to be", and that a co-founder worked much harder, partly because of clearer authority and a mentor's wisdom.
- He sees the next 3 to 6 months as his chance to turn the ship around and make Quitter ubiquitous, where "everyone knows what Quitter is".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A Miami vlog week where Alex Slater, founder of the Quitter app, shares two concrete growth levers: a Stripe web paywall that avoids Apple's cut, and raising ad spend 20% a day while profitable. He also covers bringing in an experienced investor, cutting operational waste, and choosing a high-energy location.

chunks.heading: Pricing and payments: moving US paywall traffic to Stripe to avoid Apple's fee
chunks.text:
- Alex's app, Quitter, originally monetized through Apple's in-app payment paywall.
- He built a Stripe integration so the paywall can take payment through Stripe and skip Apple's cut. He describes it as "I can now get the Stripe pay and skip Apple's fee."
- The Stripe paywall is shown only to users in the USA region.
- Rollout was a 10% test: 10% of users see the Stripe paywall. As data comes back showing it is more profitable, he plans to "introduce it to everyone."
- He compared proceeds on the transaction-abandoned paywall (Stripe versus regular Apple). Stripe proceeds are "almost double... more like 30%" higher. The gap is the fee paid to Apple that Stripe avoids.
- His takeaway is that the integration lets the business "continue scaling proceeds" and that the proceeds number "should continue to go higher" as more people get the Stripe paywall.

chunks.heading: Revenue numbers and scaling paid ads
chunks.text:
- Quitter does about $17-18k a day gross on Apple. After Apple's cut it is more like $12-13k a day in proceeds.
- Yesterday's figures: ad spend of $4.1k, about $17,000 gross and about $13,000 in proceeds.
- His scaling rule: raise ad spend 20% a day, on the condition that it remains profitable. If it stays profitable, spend steps up daily (roughly $4.1k to $4.5k to $5k to $5.5k and so on).
- Within about a week, if things go well, he expects to spend $10-20k a day. He says that would put Quitter over $1 million a month in revenue, a target he had wanted "for all of these months" and had just "figured out how to do it."
- He frames Stripe as extra upside on top of ad scaling: "with the Stripe integration, we could just go way higher."
- His ambition: if the business hit around $4 million a month while staying as profitable as it is, he thinks selling Quitter for $100 million is "not unrealistic at all."

chunks.heading: Cutting operational bloat and bringing in an experienced investor
chunks.text:
- Alex was meeting an investor (Zach) at a Coconut Grove steakhouse in Miami, with a co-founder (Connor) present, hoping to "shake hands on the spot."
- His reasoning for taking on experienced help: "it's easier for someone with more experience to come in and tell you what to focus your time on rather than you guessing and trying to figure it out yourself."
- He has no doubt the founding team (himself, Connor, Chris) could figure it out. The point is that an experienced partner would save "several months" and add liquidity to his pocket.
- After going through the Slack workspace, the business and its operations with Zach, the team realized "how much [waste] there is." Alex says it felt "relieving" to cut it out and to shut things down as soon as they pop up.
- He sees the cleanup as the unlock: considering how far the business has come, "it's scary, exciting to see where we can go after clearing it all up."

chunks.heading: Location and environment as a performance lever
chunks.text:
- Alex moved to London and, after about two months, felt restless and cut off. He concluded he wanted to stay in Miami instead.
- Reasons for Miami:
  - Creativity and opportunities "unlocked" within 24 hours of being there.
  - Fewer distractions: no school friends and no car to be pulled away by. He says he is "just focused."
  - The sun and energy make him "way more inspired" and "way more hungry."
  - Time zone: the team needs to be on East Coast time. Time zones are "a big one."
- His critique of London: everything "slows down to Porter speed" and staying would delay his "dream life by another 6 to 8 months." His line: "Why be the horse when you can be the Ferrari?"
- His plan: take meetings in New York, bring the team to Miami on an Airbnb for at least 20-30 days, go back to London for a month, then return to Miami for a fuller stint.

chunks.heading: Founder mindset: optimizing for stories and consistency
chunks.text:
- Alex's life-optimization frame is experiences, memories and stories. He imagines telling his future kids about being a young founder in Miami "closing big deals, building massive companies," and says he is "busy writing the coolest story ever."
- On motivation, he and his co-founders discussed instant gratification: people with no purpose scroll TikTok, watch "lock in" content, tell a friend "this is the year we make money," and then "don't do [anything]." His point is that the dopamine loop replaces action.
- He ended a night by finishing the Stripe setup so he could "wake up tomorrow... knowing that I did something productive," which sets up a productive next day.
- A rent discussion for a Miami team house priced at $125k a month: he argues rent should be judged as a percentage of income. At $1 million a month in income, $100k rent is about 10%, "still a lot of money," but split five ways at about $20k each it is manageable.

chunks.heading: Team and working style
chunks.text:
- The team works in person for lock-in periods. Connor and Peter were due to come to London for two months to "lock in," and the plan is to rotate the team between London and Miami.
- Alex and his co-founder Connor build and ship hands-on. He personally worked on the Stripe integration late at night in a hotel room with the team.
- He tracks nutrition and habits as part of the routine, including a calorie-tracking app (Cal AI) for macros, using ChatGPT to estimate calories and scanning barcodes where possible.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Slater reflects on going from broke to a Miami mansion in a year, building Quitter to about $500k/month. He explains the simple influencer-led app playbook, why scaling is the hard part, and how he plans to break the plateau by focusing on volume inputs and outputs.

chunks.heading: Quitter's app-building playbook: influencers, volume, and scaling past $500K/month
chunks.text:
Alex describes the model behind Quitter (a quit-pornography app) and At Mafia as a simple loop, and says the hard part is scaling, not profiting.

- **Step 1:** build an app that is valuable, that you would pay for, and that actually works.
- **Step 2:** find influencers in your niche with a cult-like following who will push the app inside their videos.
- **Step 3:** some viewers of those videos download the app, and some downloads become sales.
- **Step 4:** reinvest the sales revenue into more distribution and more influencers, and you have a business.
- He says getting to the first $30K month "genuinely wasn't difficult".
- By his account the hard part is "systemizing things" and "scaling beyond your mindset".
- Example of the margin squeeze: nine team members, about $100K a month on ads, about $500K revenue, then Apple takes 30%, leaving "a bit of that".
- His fix is to become lean and keep scaling operations.

chunks.heading: How Quitter reached about $500K a month, and why he thinks it should be more
chunks.text:
- He describes the growth as a few viral stunts plus a steady system, not one trick.
- The stunts included Quitter buying OnlyFans, which he says brought a couple hundred thousand to maybe $300K in revenue plus a lot of mind share.
- The rest was "a hell of a lot more influencers, a hell of a lot more ads" and keeping the system flowing.
- He says "it wasn't really that difficult".
- He quotes about $3.2 million in total revenue so far.
- He says the two companies he is affiliated with, At Mafia and Quitter, did $1 million combined in the last month.
- He is not satisfied: he had said he would hit higher numbers by April, May or June, but as of late September revenue was still stuck near $500K a month.
- He believes the business "should be doing" $1M to $3M a month.

chunks.heading: Inputs and outputs: the volume math for getting to $1M a month
chunks.text:
- His plan is to stop chasing the big number and go back to fundamentals: look at the inputs (volume of content) and the outputs (views, downloads, revenue).
- Current run rate is roughly $12.5K to $15K a day.
- Tripling daily volume would give about $35K to $36K a day, which adds up to roughly $1M a month.
- The target is concrete: get three days' worth of content, views, downloads and revenue into one day. He calls this "pretty simple".
- He notes the mental barrier he hit at $500K a month came from staring at the headline number instead of the daily inputs.

chunks.heading: Volume and persistence as the core principle
chunks.text:
- He cites a quote he credits to Hormozi: "do so much volume that it would be unreasonable to fail".
- His view is that if you put in real effort and don't stop until you "crack the code", you can't fail.
- His example is to treat any goal as research plus iteration. For a would-be top singer: study the rise of other artists, iterate on the beat, put out content constantly, make it catchy, post on TikTok, and obsess over it daily.
- On his own start: after his first video he did not just post it and move on. He acted on it.
- He says he was flown to San Francisco with about $5 in his bank account and "hustled".
- His advice is to set your standards much higher and think beyond money. "It's not 10k a month. It's not 100k a month. It's not driving a Lamborghini." Ask what gives you true purpose.
- He says he could rebuild his position again; it would only take time.

chunks.heading: Shifting culture instead of only selling an app
chunks.text:
- He wants people to use Quitter because culture has changed, not just because they saw an ad.
- Goal: make it cool to quit watching pornography, and make people love the mission.
- The planned vehicle is a "winter arc" update with more gamification and stronger Quitter branding.
- He frames Twitter (social media) as the best resource for that cultural shift.

chunks.heading: Org lesson: promoting an operator to CEO
chunks.text:
- He and his co-founder felt overwhelmed. They had a duty to lead a team but were distracted by lifestyle and At Mafia, and they were the bottleneck.
- They promoted an internal person who used to run ads (named Peter) to CEO.
- Peter is the one who "stepped up" and does the groundwork.
- The founders act as puppet masters: they protect the vision and quality bar, and make the key decisions.
- He says taking the founders away from daily operations lets them make better company decisions.

chunks.heading: Lesson: comfort and overpaying yourself kills output
chunks.text:
- Over the last 3 to 4 months, after he stopped making YouTube videos, he got extremely comfortable.
- He paid himself too much each month from Quitter revenue while his work output did not rise with it.
- His read is that getting paid more for doing nothing "rewires" the brain to treat doing nothing as rewarding, which wrecks motivation.
- He lost sight of the mission and thought about his next five-figure payout instead of the team, cutting costs, bringing work in-house, or improving quality.
- His fix is to get realigned on the mission and tie effort back to output.

chunks.heading: Idea: a "Super Health" ecosystem
chunks.text:
- Thesis: people increasingly care about health (he cites Whoop, cutting seed oils, Apple Watch). Quitter worked because there was a niche of men who wanted to quit pornography.
- He sees a billion-dollar opportunity in unifying health around one login, "the Apple ecosystem for health".
- The layers, from the bottom:
  - **App layer (dominate first):** own apps such as Quitter, Cali, Strava-type, MyFitnessPal-type, running and sleep apps.
  - **Physical products:** Whoop, Oura rings, Eight Sleep, Apple Watch.
  - **Supplements and food:** AG1, Blueprint.
  - **Top of the pyramid:** a Super Health profile that holds all the data in one place.
- Monetization idea: about "$39 a month" for a subscription across apps, supplements and sleep.
- He calls the idea a genius concept but "incredibly difficult to execute on".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Slater updates on Quitter after 20 days back: steady $9-10k proceeds days, rising LTV and ARPU, after he cut a 14-person team. He explains how he tests whether he is the bottleneck, works directly on paywalls and content, and holds a high bar on his own content.

chunks.heading: Quitter revenue recovered after stepping back in: team cut from 14, revenue went up
chunks.text:
- Alex stepped away from Quitter to test whether he was "the issue." His words: "spoiler, I wasn't the issue."
- 20 days after returning, the app was doing a consistent $9-10k in proceeds per day, about $15k gross revenue per day.
- His first week back produced roughly "like 140k in revenue" (the video title says $150k). The transcript wording is ambiguous, so treat the exact figure as roughly $140-150k.
- Per-user metrics were rising across the board: "ROAS, LTV, ARPU all these figures are going up and up."
- Team change: the team had 14 people, and "we fired everyone and the revenue went up. It didn't go down, it went up." He calls team roles a "big problem."
- His framing of the experiment: a founder pulling back to see whether the business runs without them is the "true test" of whether they are the bottleneck.

chunks.heading: What Alex does day to day when running Quitter
chunks.text:
- He goes "behind the scenes" and looks at the paywalls, improving them "based on what I want."
- He works on the content itself, making "content that I want to watch." His taste is the filter for what ships.
- He reviews team roles and questions whether each one is needed.
- The three levers he names are paywalls, content and team structure, not new features.

chunks.heading: Standard for content: refuses to post mediocre content
chunks.text:
- He filmed a "chapter 4" behind-the-scenes video, then didn't post it because footage of someone behind a laptop all day isn't entertaining. The edit exists; he held it back anyway.
- "I'm just not content with mediocre content." He cites this as the reason he posts rarely on Instagram and Twitter: "I want to be exceptional in every facet of life."
- He apologizes for taking 2 weeks to post, attributing it to a "very high standard."
- His target for better content is visually dynamic, high-stakes scenes rather than screen time:
  - travelling London to New York and filming behind the scenes
  - in-person meetings and whiteboard-style design sessions in a physical office
  - pulling up Quitter revenue on a Times Square billboard
  - packing presents for friends before flying to London
  - the build and launch of his new app, Reset
- He sums it up as wanting "constant exhilaration" in what he produces.

chunks.heading: Content system: a second "diary" channel for lower-grade material
chunks.text:
- He launched a second YouTube channel, "Alex Slater's Diary," for random thoughts that aren't good enough for the main channel.
- It works as a dump for unpolished material, so the main channel can keep a high bar without losing the rest.
- Example of what goes there: a 40-minute 3am ramble covering a wide range of topics.

chunks.heading: Next product: Reset
chunks.text:
- He is working on a new app called Reset, "about to launch."
- He says money is "coming back in" and he feels grateful.
- No pricing, mechanics or launch tactics are given in this source.

chunks.heading: Mindset on setbacks
chunks.text:
- Looking back at the video he made two weeks earlier during the low point, he says he "always knew I'd be fine."
- His belief: "when you're meant to be great, you will find something great to achieve and you will do it regardless of the circumstances."
- His sign-off principles: "always grind, always hustle, never give up, don't procrastinate. Just become the best you." He says that is "the only thing that you will get respect for."
